news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy's Odds of Winning in Ohio Hit All-Time Low: What Polls Show
news.text: Republican candidate for Ohio Governor Vivek Ramaswamy's odds of winning the race against Democrat Amy Acton dipped to a new low on prediction market site Kalshi on Monday as the race for the governor's mansion heats up before midterms. According to the prediction market site, Ramaswamy's odds in April fell below Acton's before surging at the end of May. He again trailed Acton around August 13, and has not rebounded since. Kalshi on Monday posted to X that Ramaswamy's odds of 43 percent marked his new all-time overall low. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during midterm elections. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. President Donald Trump won Ohio in the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris by double digits and he has backed Ramaswamy, also a candidate for the White House two years ago, in his bid for the governor's seat. Newsweek reached out to both Acton and Ramaswamy's campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know Ramaswamy and Acton, a physician who previously led Ohio's Department of Health, face off as GOP Governor Mike DeWine is term-limited. Although Ohio twice voted for former President Barack Obama, in 2008 and 2012, the state has recently trended Republican in election cycles, backing Trump in three consecutive presidential contests. Democrats also suffered a notable loss in the last election when longtime Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown lost his bid for another term to Republican Bernie Moreno. Even so, Democrats see Ohio as one of their best pickup opportunities in the 2026 midterms. In addition to the governor's race, the party is eyeing Brown's Senate comeback attempt against Republican Senator Jon Husted. Recent surveys have also seemingly pointed to close contests, with Acton and Brown often holding slim leads. The Cook Political Report rates the Ohio Senate election contest as a toss-up. Democrats hope to capitalize on Trump's unfavorable polling as his overall approval rating hits record lows as well as key administrative policies like immigration, the economy and foreign policy amid the ongoing war with Iran. Prediction market site Polymarket gives Acton a 58 percent chance of winning compared to Ramaswamy's 41 percent. On the site, Acton has led her Republican opponent since late August. Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Monday, "A drop for Ramaswamy on Kalshi is worth watching because Ohio should be friendly terrain for a Republican. When traders put Acton near 57 to 59 percent, they are pricing in a midterm environment that is tougher for the party in power, plus questions about Ramaswamy’s personal standing with independents." "It is concerning as a signal, not as a verdict. Parties look at prediction markets more than they did a few years ago, especially operatives and donors who want a live scoreboard. They do not treat them as a true snapshot of the electorate. Markets reflect money, news flow and trader bias. Polls, turnout models and field work still decide how campaigns spend. Use Kalshi as an early warning, not as a substitute for voters. Sites like PredictionEdge.com are becoming more popular for political prediction markets." What Polling Shows A YouGov and Bowling Green State University poll this month shows that 48 percent would pick Acton over 45 percent who said Ramaswamy in Ohio's gubernatorial race. Four percent said Libertarian Don Kissick and 3 percent chose someone else. When asked regardless of preference, who they think will win the race, 62 percent said Ramaswamy, 36 percent said Acton and 1 percent said Kissick. The poll surveyed 1,000 likely Ohio voters from September 1 to September 10 and had a margin of error of 4 percent. A Wedgewood poll shows Acton up 1 percent, with 48 percent compared to Ramaswamy's 47 percent and 7 percent are undecided. The poll surveyed 800 likely voters from August 11 to August 13 and has a 4 percent margin of error. Ramaswamy leads in a Fox News Poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, with 50 percent compared to Acton's 48 percent. The poll shows a shift from June, when Acton was up 1 point with 50 percent compared to Ramaswamy's 49 percent. The poll also shows that Ramaswamy's favorability rating is 46 percent compared to a 44 percent unfavorable rating. Acton's favorability rating is 43 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating. The poll was conducted from August 6 to August 10 among 1,008 Ohio registered voters and had a margin of error of 3 percent. According to the Cook Political Report, the race is also rated as a toss-up. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Although Ohio voted for former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, the state has recently trended Republican.

news.title: The Real Reason Why Democrats Won’t Denounce the Socialists
news.text:

Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany laid out just how far this has gone during a discussion on The Five, and the reason why Democrats aren’t nipping this problem in the bud.

"These DSA-ers are winning all across the country, and they're making a huge insurgency that is not going away," McEnany said. "It is going to get stronger." news.title: Susan Collins Warns Trump on NIH Grant Plan as Polls Show Tight Maine Race
news.text: Senator Susan Collins is warning the Trump administration against what she describes as an effort to politicize federal health research funding, escalating a dispute over control of National Institutes of Health (NIH) grants as she faces a reelection race that recent polling suggests could be one of the most competitive of her career. The Maine Republican's criticism comes as recent polling shows Democrat Troy Jackson holding a narrow edge in the race for Collins' Senate seat. A CNN/SSRS poll released earlier this month found Jackson leading Collins 48 percent to 45 percent, while other recent surveys have also pointed to a highly competitive contest. The race is rated a toss-up by major election forecasters. The dispute erupted after The Washington Post reported Friday that President Donald Trump is considering an executive order that would create a commission to review NIH grants, potentially giving political appointees a role in determining how the agency distributes nearly $50 billion in biomedical research funding. The Post reported that White House budget chief Russell Vought led criticism of the NIH, arguing the agency had funded "woke" initiatives that conflicted with Trump's priorities and should face additional scrutiny. Newsweek reached out to the White House, NIH, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and Collins' office for comment on Monday afternoon. Collins Challenges White House In a statement posted Monday, Collins argued that the Trump administration would be crossing a line if it moved forward with the proposal. "The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) should not be involved in agency decisions on the awards of grants," Collins wrote on X. She added that "any attempt to politicize grantmaking at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), or any other agency, by another means, whether an Executive Order or guidance, is contrary to congressional intent." Collins further warned that political review of grants already vetted by scientists would undermine the existing process. "Imposing a political review on awards that have already been selected through a rigorous scientific and merit-based process undermines the long-standing principle that the government funds awards based on scientific need and merit, rather than political ideology." Her statement came after congressional leaders from both parties raised concerns about the reported effort. The Washington Post reported Monday that Collins, Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Patty Murray and House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro all warned against giving the White House additional control over NIH grant decisions. Grant Fight Started Months Ago Collins' opposition to the latest proposal did not begin this month. In a July 6 letter to Vought, the Senate Appropriations Committee chair urged OMB to withdraw portions of a proposed government-wide grant-making rule and extend its comment period. Collins argued that parts of the proposal would undermine scientific and biomedical research, create burdens for small communities and conflict with Congress' authority over federal spending. At the center of her concerns was a provision that would have required senior political appointees to conduct an additional review of grants after they had already completed scientific and merit-based evaluation. The proposal directed appointees to consider whether awards "demonstrably advance the President's policy priorities" and use their "independent judgment" when reviewing funding decisions. Collins warned at the time that political review could shift decisions away from scientific merit and toward ideological considerations. She also objected to provisions allowing federal agencies to terminate discretionary grants if officials determined they no longer aligned with agency priorities or the national interest. In her July letter, Collins warned that abruptly ending federal awards could have serious consequences for long-term medical studies and patients participating in research. "For example, the termination of clinical trials would leave patients without treatment and could well result in significant scientific and financial losses to both the recipient and the Federal government," she wrote. She added that uncertainty over potential grant cancellations could discourage researchers and institutions from pursuing multiyear federally funded studies. That history helps explain why Collins viewed the reported executive-order effort as a continuation of the same grant-making fight she had been waging against OMB for months. Oval Office Clash Reported The controversy intensified after reports of a tense Oval Office meeting involving Trump, Vought and NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, who leads the nation's largest single funder of biomedical research. According to The Washington Post, Vought argued that NIH continued funding projects that conflicted with Trump's agenda and proposed additional oversight of grant-making. Bhattacharya reportedly defended the agency's current review process during the meeting. In comments reported by The New York Times, NIH spokesman Joshua Pradko declined to discuss details of the meeting but said the agency remained committed to funding biomedical research. Pradko also pushed back on suggestions that NIH grant funding could be pulled back, saying: "There will be no rescissions to NIH grant monies. All NIH grant monies will be spent." The comments suggested NIH leaders are continuing to resist efforts to pull back congressionally approved research funding. The Times subsequently reported that administration officials were drafting an order that could establish an outside committee empowered to review or potentially veto grants viewed as inconsistent with administration priorities. The reported proposal follows months of friction between OMB and NIH. Vought has repeatedly criticized grants he considers "woke" and has argued political officials should have greater authority to review federal spending decisions. Bhattacharya, while supporting efforts to eliminate what he considers ideologically driven research, has also publicly pledged that NIH would spend the funding appropriated by Congress. Congress included language in a continuing resolution signed into law earlier this month that temporarily blocks implementation of OMB's proposed grant-making rule through December 11. In Monday's statement, Collins argued that any attempt to achieve a similar outcome through "an Executive Order or guidance" would be contrary to congressional intent. Bipartisan Opposition Emerges Lawmakers from both parties criticized the reported proposal. "Whether lifesaving medical research gets funded or not should be determined by experts at the NIH, not a panel of lackeys chosen by Donald Trump and Russ Vought," Murray said in a statement shared with Newsweek. She warned that "a single political appointee could kill a cancer study or an Alzheimer's trial with no scientific reason at all." Murray also accused Trump of attempting to use scientific funding decisions to advance political goals. "Only one question should decide which research gets funded: is this good science that could save lives? Trump wants to answer a different question: does this help me settle a score?" She called on Republicans to oppose any effort to politicize medical research funding, "whether that's an OMB rule or a new executive order." Maine Race Remains Tight The NIH dispute arrives as Collins navigates a difficult political environment. Recent polling has consistently pointed to a competitive race between Collins and Jackson. The CNN/SSRS survey found Collins with a 41 percent favorable rating and a 51 percent unfavorable rating, while Jackson registered a 36 percent favorable rating and a 42 percent unfavorable rating. The same survey found that 67 percent of Mainers disapprove of Trump, compared with 31 percent who approve. A Fox News survey found Jackson ahead by 2 points, while a University of New Hampshire poll showed him leading by 3 points. An Abacus Data poll found Jackson ahead 52 percent to 43 percent among likely voters, although Collins held a narrow 46 percent to 45 percent edge among all registered voters. Those figures underscore the challenge Republicans face in Maine, a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024. Still, Collins has repeatedly proved resilient. In 2020, she won reelection despite trailing Democrat Sara Gideon in most public polling and Maine's backing of the Democratic presidential nominee. For questions about this story, contact Newsweek editor Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: The Republican senator is pushing back on a reported Trump administration effort to increase political oversight of NIH grants.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Accused of 'Messing with Kamala Harris' Head' After California Gov Claims He Won't Run for Prez If She Does
news.text:
Gavin Newsom says he would step aside from a potential 2028 presidential bid for former Vice President Kamala Harris, but his media tour around Southern states tells a different story, Radar Online has learned. 

Whether Newsom ultimately runs or sits out the Democratic primary, his second term as governor of California is coming to an end, and his recent political activity suggests he is preparing for a future that requires a national audience.Will Gavin Newsom Run for Office?The Daily Mail reported that Newsom’s pledge to defer to Harris has raised questions among Democratic strategists about whether the move is as straightforward as it appears. A former Harris adviser told the outlet, "I think he's messing with her, getting in her head.

Another Democratic strategist said the pledge could create a "him vs. her" dynamic and potentially isolate Harris from donors.

Newsom has already stepped into the national spotlight through his political tour of the South. He traveled through Alabama, North Carolina, and South Carolina on his "Take It Back" tour, with South Carolina receiving the most attention because it is scheduled to host the first Democratic presidential primary of the 2028 cycle.

The San Francisco Chronicle described the trip as a test run for a potential presidential campaign. Newsom held multiple events in South Carolina, appeared on PBS and other media platforms, and met with Democratic figures as he tested his message outside California. Rep. Jim Clyburn, a powerful South Carolina Democrat, also met with Newsom and later said he felt "good about his chances."Kamala Harris V. Gavin Newsom?Newsom has also acknowledged that a primary fight against Harris could hurt both candidates because they share voters, supporters, and donors. Speaking with CNN's Jake Tapper, Newsom called a potential contest between the two Californians "mutual assured destruction."

As Radar previously reported, Newsom has expressed interest in a presidential bid while leaving his 2028 plans open. 

Harris has also not announced whether she will run again after losing the 2024 presidential election to Republican Donald Trump.Is Gavin Newsom Testing the Waters?The Daily Mail also reported that some Democrats believe Newsom could benefit politically from appearing deferential to Harris. One strategist told the outlet that if Harris does not run, Newsom could receive credit with Black voters for stepping aside and potentially gain Harris’ endorsement.

Meanwhile, Harris has continued to signal that she is considering another presidential campaign. 

Harris' recent appearances and focus on South Carolina, where Black voters make up a large portion of the Democratic primary electorate.

news.title: Nikole Hannah-Jones May Have Just Written a Eulogy for Woke Idealism
news.text: Ten years ago, Pulitzer Prize winner Nikole Hannah-Jones, best known for creating The 1619 Project, which examines the legacy of slavery in America, put her daughter on the cover of The New York Times Magazine to make a case for school integration that was also deeply personal: If you believe in integrated schools, what happens when the choice is your own child’s education? “I worried — I worry still — about whether I made the right decision for our little girl. But I knew I made the just one,” Hannah-Jones wrote in her 2016 essay after Najya, her daughter, was accepted into a high-poverty Brooklyn school that she and her husband had chosen. Najya ended up at Public School 307, whose attendance zone was drawn closely around the Farragut Houses, a large public housing development. At the time, 91 percent of its students were Black and Latino. In a sequel published in the same magazine over the weekend, Hannah-Jones revisited the decision years later and acknowledged that she might have gotten it wrong. Newsweek reached out to Hannah-Jones for comment on Monday. What Hannah-Jones Actually Admits in the New Essay The admission isn't just that the school failed. It's that Hannah-Jones knew there were problems, kept going anyway, and now says she cannot forgive herself for what that decision meant for her daughter. “When it comes to the choices my husband and I have made about public education, these days I feel that I failed both my values and my child,” she writes. She goes further than regret. Describing the moment she understood what nine years of emails and unanswered complaints had cost Najya, she writes: “I felt overcome with regret. Najya deserved better. They all did. But she was mine. This girl, my only child, looked to me to protect her, to give her what she needed to thrive. And I had not chosen her.” Hannah-Jones had spent years reporting on the ways public schools fail children. She and her husband also had a choice about where to send their own daughter. She now writes that they made the wrong choice for Najya. The consequences became clear over time. Najya was one of the brightest students in her class, Hannah-Jones writes, but she still could not pass the state algebra exam. Years later, after struggling with algebra gaps that a tutor traced back to elementary school, Najya told her mother: “I never really got the education I wanted.” Then she asked a question that forced Hannah-Jones to confront the decision itself: “Did you know my school was bad like this when you decided to put me here?” Hannah-Jones describes finding her daughter's math folder filled with ungraded assignments. “None of them were graded,” she writes, adding that most of the answers were wrong. A school literacy coach later told her that Najya's teacher had “most likely never performed the school's mandatory reading assessments for Najya or any of her classmates.” The failures had accumulated over years. So had the complaints. Hannah-Jones writes that she eventually understood how much her daughter had been struggling and how long she had been missing the education she needed. “I almost cannot type the words,” she writes, recalling an image of Najya as a young girl in cornrows and a school uniform. “Because when I do... the tears come.” When she apologized to her daughter, she kept it simple. “I acknowledge to you that I didn't do the best for you, and I am so sorry.” She continues to defend the larger argument behind her views on public education. In the same essay, she writes that Black students remain the most segregated group in New York's schools and that the country has “actually moved backward” on integration since 2016. The Backlash: Woke 1.0 on Trial Within hours, the essay was being read as more than a personal reckoning. It became part of a broader debate over “Woke 1.0,” a term coined by New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé's, and widely used on social media to describe the progressive politics that shaped the years from roughly 2017 through the George Floyd protests and the pandemic. Henry Mack, Florida's education commissioner and former U.S. assistant secretary of labor under President Donald Trump, framed the essay as evidence that the sacrifice never had a payoff. "Nikole Hannah-Jones got a MacArthur 'genius' grant and a magazine cover for putting her daughter in a failing school as a civic sacrament. Ten years later the kid can't do fractions, failed the algebra exam after collecting A's, and asked her mother why other children's disadvantage mattered more than her own education. That's not integration. That's a byline with a body count of one," he wrote on X. Maud Maron, a Manhattan public defender and former New York City Council candidate who has spent nearly a decade fighting to preserve the Specialized High School Admissions Test, made the argument personal in a different direction. Hannah-Jones had once interviewed her for the 2016 essay and, in Maron's telling, dismissed her defense of the exam as racist. "I knew then what she has just figured out," Maron wrote, "that her identitarian race-based grievance project would not fix anything. And in fact, it has hurt all public-school students." Maron's sharpest criticism was about the kind of school Najya eventually chose. The high school she attended uses screened admissions, a model that has been part of New York's broader debate over school segregation and selective admissions. Maron argued that Hannah-Jones' daughter was able to benefit from a system Hannah-Jones had criticized in her own work and advocacy. “Your daughter's chosen high school would not exist but for parents like me who fought so hard to keep screened schools,” Maron wrote. “Unlike Hannah-Jones I have nothing to walk back,” she added. Not every reaction was hostile. Monica Marks, professor of Middle East politics at NYU Abu Dhabi who writes frequently for the Times, praised Hannah-Jones on X for the candor itself. "Humanism that values people as individuals seems preferable to vicarious activism that views loved ones as vehicles. Good on Hannah-Jones for writing this candid op-ed. She must have known she'd take heat for it, but decided to confront herself in print anyway. Not easy to do." Which Progressives Have Walked Back Their 2020 Positions? The phrase “Woke 1.0” has drawn national attention in recent months as several progressive candidates have revisited past statements and positions, including calls to defund the police, identity politics, opposition to school admissions screens and gifted programs, and the language that came with those debates. In August, New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was asked on ABC’s This Week about some of the past statements made by progressive candidates running this year. “I have a local city councilman that has this saying, ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’” she said, adding that what matters is what a candidate says now. Ocasio-Cortez went on to suggest that the pandemic period had pushed Democrats to consider a wide range of ideas, and that some of the rhetoric from that period was not language she would use today. She did not say the underlying ideas had been wrong. “I actually think that the discussions that were had at that time were quite fruitful,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different from the way we talked about crime and bringing crime down.” The pattern has now spread across the Democratic field. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Senate candidate in Michigan, deleted scores of posts supporting defunding the police and has since said he rejects the idea. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani apologized during his campaign for 2020 posts describing the New York Police Department as racist and a threat to public safety, then kept Jessica Tisch as police commissioner, a decision that drew criticism from some of his allies on the left. Darializa Avila Chevalier, who won the Democratic primary in New York's 13th Congressional District, also faced scrutiny over thousands of old social media posts. During the campaign, she said she regretted some of what she had written, including a 2021 attack on then-Vice President Kamala Harris. “What I said was just wrong. That was not fair to her,” she said. Asked about Ossé's comment that “Woke 1 was crazy,” Avila Chevalier agreed: “Woke 1 was indeed crazy.” She said progressives can lose sight of their broader goals when they spend too much time trying to show who is “more progressive” or “more woke,” arguing that this kind of rhetoric can create divisions within the movement. In Arizona, congressional candidate JoAnna Mendoza has spent the campaign explaining a 2020 answer about shifting some police funding to social programs. The questions have extended beyond policing to immigration enforcement, school discipline, transgender participation in sports and the diversity programs that expanded after 2020. There have also been casualties. Francesca Hong lost the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin after facing sustained scrutiny over old posts and comments. In 2020, she wrote, “Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621,” and called it a “colonizer holiday.” During the campaign, she told Newsweek she had changed her views. She also faced questions about past calls to defund and abolish the police. “"The governor cannot defund the police, and I won't defund the police," she said. What Comes Next With less than 1 1/2 months before the midterm election, dozens of progressive candidates are on the ballot, and Democrats are still debating how much of the politics associated with the past decade should remain part of the party's message. Some Democrats are urging candidates to focus more heavily on economic issues. House Democrats have already put much of their focus on affordability. Hakeem Jeffries, House minority leader, has made the cost of living, healthcare costs, groceries and other household expenses central to the party's 2026 message. Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at Third Way, told Newsweek that the electability argument is still the one to focus on. "The winning Democrat will be a pugnacious centrist," Kessler said, describing a candidate who pairs institutional reform with kitchen-table economics rather than the identity-driven framing he said defined the party's approach in 2020. That debate is also showing up around transgender athletes in sports, one of the most damaging attack lines that Democrats faced during the 2024 election cycle. James Talarico in Texas, Marcy Kaptur in Ohio, Lindsay James in Iowa and Josh Turek in Iowa have all addressed the issue directly, releasing ads or making statements opposing the participation of transgender athletes in women's sports. The shift comes as polling shows that this position is shared by a majority of voters. In a 2025 Gallup poll, 69 percent of Americans said transgender athletes should only be allowed to compete on sports teams that match their sex at birth, while 24 percent said they should be allowed to compete on teams matching their gender identity. Among Democrats, 45 percent supported allowing transgender athletes to compete according to their gender identity, down from 55 percent in 2021. news.title: Trump and the GOP lose a key edge with voters: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into our newest poll to underscore the challenge facing Republicans at the polls this fall. Plus, Natasha Korecki and Matt Dixon examine Elon Musk’s under-the-radar midterm role (so far). — Adam Wollner Trump and the GOP lose a key edge with voters Analysis by Sahil Kapur Ever since he first descended down a golden escalator in 2015, President Donald Trump and his party have possessed a powerful political asset: Voters have generally trusted them on the economy. But that appears to be shifting heading into the November midterm elections.Our new NBC News poll released over the weekend found that 39% registered voters trust Democrats more to handle the economy, compared to 38% who trusted Republicans more — a 1-point difference. While voters have been split relatively evenly on the issue between the two parties in recent NBC News polling, Republicans had long held an edge on the question. Republicans had a 15-point advantage in October 2018 — one month before Democrats gained a net of 41 seats to win control of the House — and a 19-point advantage in September 2022. The only other time during the Trump era Democrats led on the question of which party voters trust more on the economy was in December 2017. [chart] Similarly, the latest NBC News poll showed that 55% of registered voters said that Trump’s policies have “hurt” the economy, while 26% say they’ve “helped.” That net margin of negative 29 points is 16 points worse than Trump performed on the issue in a March NBC News poll. And in September 2018, voters said 41%-26% that Trump’s policies had helped the economy, rather than hurt. Inflation and the cost of living topped the list of voters’ most important issues facing the country in the new poll (28%), while another 9% said jobs and the economy. The issue of the economy has powered Trump in his own presidential bids. Most recently, in 2024, 53% of voters said they trusted Trump more to handle the economy, according to exit polls, while 46% chose Kamala Harris. That year, voters who rated the economy as their No. 1 issue preferred Trump over Harris by an eye-popping 81%-18%. But two years later, voters have soured on Trump and the GOP amid the ongoing Iran war and stubbornly high prices at the gas pump and grocery store. It’s deprived the party of an asset that has tended to shield them even when the chips were down, heading into an election where they are trying to hang on to control of both chambers of Congress. 🗳️ More from the NBC News poll: Voters recoil at candidates who back data center construction, by Scott BlandFewer Democrats plan to vote by mail in the midterms, by Jane C. Timm Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans want to keep it that way. By Natasha Korecki and Matt Dixon The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court race. He donned a cheesehead, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest. In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration. Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling. But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help. Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events. And privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen GOP strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million to boost Donald Trump and his party. Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. Read more → 📊 Survey says: A new NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll on the Texas Senate race showed James Talarico at 46% and Ken Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Another 8% of potential voters were still up for grabs. Meanwhile, in the Texas governor’s race, the poll found GOP Gov. Greg Abbott at 48% and Democrat Gina Hinojosa at 41%. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

news.title: Go inside Israel's war room on the day Hamas invaded
news.text:
In July 2024, when the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, visited presidential candidate Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago, Netanyahu was pictured presenting Trump with a baseball cap that said “Total Victory.”

It was a reference not to Trump’s electoral hopes but to Israel’s war aims following the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack. Israel demanded the return of all the kidnapped hostages. It also sought the elimination of the Hamas terrorist organization in Gaza. And it wanted to extinguish the capability of Hamas, or of any other terrorist organization, to launch another Oct. 7-style surprise attack on Israel.

Nearly three years after Oct. 7, 2023, it’s easy to forget all the subsequent twists and turns. One great achievement of “In the War Room: The Inside Story of Israel’s Fight Against Hamas and the Iranian Axis,” by Yonah Jeremy Bob and Elliot Kaufman, is reminding readers of all the victories Israel has achieved since the day of the attack.

Even readers who have followed the war closely may find themselves cheered to recall that during a few days in December 2024, after Bashar Assad’s Iran-allied regime in Syria was toppled, “Israel destroyed the major assets of the Syrian military: Chemical weapons, air-defense batteries, combat aircraft, helicopters, drones, the naval fleet, weapons stockpiles, production facilities, and even tanks.” 

In only two days, “Israel carried out 480 strikes, wiping out an estimated 70 percent of Syria’s strategic capabilities. A Syrian rebel commander told the Syria Direct news outlet that it would take decades to rebuild the Syrian army.”

In Gaza, Israel killed Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar. It killed Yahya Sinwar’s brother, Mohammed Sinwar, who took over Hamas in Gaza after his brother died. It killed Hamas’s military chief, Mohammed Deif. It killed the Hamas political bureau chief, Ismail Haniyeh, while Haniyeh was staying in a Tehran guesthouse that the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps used for visiting dignitaries.

In Lebanon, Israel killed the military chief of the Hezbollah terrorist group, Fuad Shukr. It killed the overall leader of Hezbollah, Hassan Nasrallah, in Beirut “alongside around twenty Hezbollah military commanders.” 

Israel killed “3,851 Hezbollah terrorists and wounded around 9,000 more,” the book reports, citing the Israel Defense Force and recounting the story of the exploding pagers. Also killed: “more than twenty-two thousand Hamas fighters.”

On the Iranian front, the US and Israel jointly significantly set back the nuclear program and killed the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, “and nearly all of his top IRGC and military commanders.” Israel killed Iran’s top two military commanders, Hossein Salami and Mohammad Bagheri. Israel killed IRGC Air Force Commander Amir Ali Hajizadeh. Israel killed the IRGC intelligence chief, Mohammad Kazemi, and his deputy.

And Israel brought back from Gaza 168 live hostages and 87 bodies of dead hostages, accounting for all those known to have been kidnapped.

Alongside the highlight reel of Israeli and American accomplishments, this book provides a kind of supercut of retrospectively ridiculous things that Israeli and American politicians have said along the way. The compilation, in one volume, of all these gems is another public service provided by Bob, who is The Jerusalem Post’s senior military analyst, and by Kaufman, who is an editorial board member of The Wall Street Journal. 

Israeli politician Benny Gantz bragged to an interviewer in 2018 that as Israel Defense Force chief of staff he had “prioritized cyber and intelligence over infantry and armor,” because “unlike the threat of ground invasion, the threat of cyber is realistic.” 

John Kerry, as President Obama’s secretary of state, cited the Afghan army to the Israelis as a model for Palestinian security forces and “an example of how local forces could be trained successfully.” 

Kamala Harris, before Israel’s invasion of the southern Gazan city of Rafah: “I have studied the maps,” she said, incorrectly claiming there was nowhere for civilians to evacuate to.

Jake Sullivan, Biden’s national security adviser, who has since landed at the Harvard Kennedy School, where he is Kissinger Professor of the Practice of Statecraft and World Order, had written a Foreign Affairs essay “that went to print just before the October 7 attack and arrived in subscribers’ mailboxes later in the month,” boasting that Biden’s policies made the Middle East “quieter than it has been for decades.” He claimed credit for having “de-escalated crises in Gaza” and having “enhanced deterrence” to discourage Iranian aggression.

The book details differences among Netanyahu, his war cabinet members Gantz and Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and Israel Defense Force chief of staff Herzi Halevi. Those internal discussions — and the parallel dialogues with the Biden and Trump administrations — shaped the outcomes in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran. The personalities also reflected the span of public opinion in Israel’s diverse democracy.

The authors are less sure-footed when analyzing US and global sentiment. “Widespread destruction became a key driver of Israel’s diminished global standing,” the authors contend. “Videos of Gazan neighborhoods turned to rubble, with nothing left intact for as far as the eye could see, told a story of their own.” And, “a young generation’s first impression of the Jewish state has been formed by the destruction of Gaza.” 

Somehow the US bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and of Dresden, didn’t diminish America’s global standing for the young generation during or after World War II. Any erosion can be blamed not on the destruction of Gaza but on a sophisticated social-media and on-the-ground campaign by foreign actors to demonize Israel, coupled with social trends in America such as declining church attendance, a flood of Muslim immigration and biblical illiteracy.

The weakest part of the book is an author’s note from Yonah Jeremy Bob. Here, Bob claims Netanyahu “harmed Israel’s name with US Democrats and other parts of the fair-minded West (Germany is another notable example) by continuing the war for too long.”

He goes on: “Whether the war should have ended in late summer 2024, early 2025 or summer 2025 is hotly debated within the Israeli defense establishment. But close to zero of the Israeli defense establishment supported continuing the war beyond that point, and beyond that point is where Israel’s standing took the largest global walloping.” 

This timeline does not cohere. It was only in October of 2025 that Hamas agreed to disarm and to return all the Israeli hostages, dead and alive. Count me as skeptical that Israel’s global standing would have been improved had the Jewish state ended the war prematurely, without getting the hostages back and without a plan to disarm and dislodge Hamas. And the sniping by the “Israeli defense establishment” against Netanyahu, an unfortunate feature of Israel’s domestic political landscape, is the rare Israeli export that America might indeed be better off boycotting.

So skip that section and appreciate the rest of the fast-paced narrative. Rerun the dramatic details of how Israel killed all those terrorists, and laugh along the way at Kerry, Sullivan and Harris. The victory may not be entirely total, but for Israel and America it’s already been quite an impressive win, especially considering how grimly this round began. And the war is not fully over quite yet.

Ira Stoll is a senior writer at the Washington Free Beacon.

news.title: Family tied to suspected Chinese spy gave $4.4M to Newsom, Calif. politicians
news.text:
A California family gave over $4.4 million in political donations to Governor Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris and other leading California politicians. And now, that family's alleged past links to infamous suspected honeypot spy Fang Fang, also known as Christine Fang, and other Chinese government officials have thrust them into an ongoing debate over foreign influence in American politics.

The Yin family made millions running McDonald's franchises in the Golden State — and became prolific donors to politicians, according to state and federal campaign records. Newly released FBI files about Fang describe the family patriarch Chei Chen Yin, commonly known by his initials "C.C.", as a one-time professional associate of Fang through an organization he founded.

And national security experts tasked with protecting U.S. institutions from infiltration by the Chinese government say they have documented alleged interactions between C.C. Yin's brother, Henry Yin, and the foreign influence wing of the Chinese government, the United Front.

Interactions between wealthy business leaders with direct ties to China have come under heavier scrutiny in recent years, as a series of scandals have erupted over alleged Chinese influence agents gaining access to elected officials from small town mayors to members of Congress and the governor of New York. Those relationships have often been facilitated with political donations.

Jacqueline Deal, a board member of State Armor, a company that helps lawmakers detect foreign influence operations, told CBS News that the Chinese government has a "broad-reaching, coordinated strategy for dominance that relies on shaping U.S. policy so that over time we get weaker and [China] gets stronger."

She said she suspects political donations are being used to help "disincentivize these leaders from noticing Chinese Communist Party political interference." There is no evidence the Yins have been co-opted in this way.

C.C. Yin told CBS News: "I love America, and I strongly condemn any effort by any foreign government to interfere in American politics or undermine our democracy." Henry Yin did not respond to requests for comment.

Yin family donated millions to political causes

C.C. Yin, 89, is known in Northern California for his philanthropy and rags-to-riches story of a Chinese immigrant arriving to the U.S. in the 1960s with just $100 and building a successful franchise business. 

He and his brother Henry Yin founded and ran an organization called Asian Pacific American Public Affairs, or APAPA, organizing support for favored political candidates and helping place interns and advisers in the offices of local, state and federal officials, according to APAPA's website.

C.C. Yin told CBS News he started APAPA to help "young people and community members develop leadership skills, understand how government works, vote, serve their communities, and participate in our democracy."

"When this country gives us opportunity, we have a responsibility to give back," he said.

Some of the Yins' giving has come in the form of large political donations.

The family has donated nearly $3 million to state-level California political causes and an additional $1,455,027 to federal campaigns, directly and through C.C. Yin's McDonald's franchise business, according to state and Federal Election Commission records.

This includes $364,817 in donations to past campaigns supporting Gavin Newsom, $80,000 to his 2019 inauguration committee and $50,000 to a nonprofit at Newsom's direction.

The Yins as individuals and C.C. Yin's McDonald's franchise also gave California Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis' campaigns $221,700 between 2018 and 2025, state records show. Former Vice President Kamala Harris' campaigns received $214,300 between 2019 and 2024, and former state Treasurer John Chiang's campaigns received $115,680.

Links to suspected spy Fang Fang

FBI files declassified by the White House in August point to a previous close working relationship between C.C. Yin and suspected Chinese spy Fang "Christine" Fang, who had a sexual relationship with disgraced former California congressman Eric Swalwell before fleeing to China in 2015.

The files include Swalwell's interviews with the FBI in 2015 and 2016, in which he identified Fang as his "point of contact" for APAPA. In one interview Swalwell said a top APAPA official directed him to Fang, according to the files. That official's name is redacted in the report, but two sources familiar with its content told CBS News it is C.C. Yin.

Fang appeared alongside C.C. Yin and Henry Yin at a 15-person APAPA event, in a photo posted on Facebook in 2013 by a City of Cupertino official.

APAPA president Kris Concepcion told CBS News that "current leadership is not aware of Fang Fang ever holding an official role with the national organization."

"Our understanding is that she was associated with a local chapter that is no longer operational," he said. "Like hundreds, or even thousands, of other community members who attend public events, being photographed with APAPA members does not mean she was an officer, board member, employee or representative of APAPA."

No evidence has emerged that Henry Yin or C.C. Yin knew about Fang's alleged espionage during her involvement in APAPA.

Chinese government meetings

After noticing APAPA's connection with Fang Fang, Deal dug into the background of Henry Yin, who previously served as national board chair of APAPA and is currently a board member.

She found a string of Chinese media reports of his attendance at 10 events in China hosted by officials from the Chinese government and its foreign influence wing, the United Front, since 2013. The United Front published Chinese-language write-ups of Henry Yin's reported meetings in 2015 and 2023.

Henry Yin has described his efforts as "networking." Deal said his relationship with China "seems to be one of open cooperation."

One article said Yin traveled to Baoshan in Yunnan province in June 2015 and held talks with the Municipal Party Committee United Front Work Department, reaching "a consensus on further strengthening contacts." It described Yin as their "designated contact person for California–China economic, trade, scientific and technological interaction".

Another 2013 article by a Chinese government office described a meeting between Yin and a Chinese government official in Chengdu, capital of Sichuan province, saying that he had been offered a position there with the title "Overseas Talent Recruitment Adviser for Sichuan Province." There is no evidence Yin accepted that offer, which was made during a friendlier time in U.S.-China relations. 

A United Front statement from 2023 said a delegation of "Chinese Entrepreneurs from Silicon Valley" including Henry Yin, visited his hometown of Chengdu and "built a new bridge for investment cooperation between Chengdu and Silicon Valley."

Henry Yin told the East Bay Times in 2016, while he was serving on the California Commission for Economic Development, that his goal was to further business relations between China and the U.S., as part of his decades as a trans-national entrepreneur.

"I've done a lot of networking, and these days I'm glad to see these networks deliver results," he told the newspaper.

Neither Henry Yin nor his brother have been accused by U.S. law enforcement of working as a foreign agent or acting against American interests.

Foreign Policy Research Institute fellow and University of Miami professor June Teufel Dreyer told CBS News that, although political donations and advisory roles are patterns of influence used by the United Front, those actions and traveling to China for diplomacy and business trips could be entirely innocent.

"There's really nothing wrong with successful Chinese entrepreneurs wanting to help out the economies of the country they originally came from," Dreyer said, but added: "We should get rid of the idea that there's such a thing as a truly private business in China. They are all controlled at some level by the government."

Cheryl Yu, a fellow at foreign affairs think tank The Jamestown Foundation, told CBS News that the Chinese government attempts to exert influence on well-connected Americans, regardless of those individuals' intentions.

"This is how the United Front works. They build these friendly, long-term relationships, then at some point they make requests," she said.

The U.S. government has allegedly engaged in its own influence attempts against China, including a clandestine social media campaign to turn public opinion in China against President Xi Jinping's government, a 2024 Reuters report claimed.

Concepcion said his organization has "no relationship with the People's Republic of China, the Chinese Communist Party, or the United Front," and that "personal travel, relationships, employment histories, and views" of members "should not be attributed to APAPA."

Top political contacts

The Yins' foreign and domestic connections have at times placed them at the nexus of Chinese diplomacy and American politics.

C.C. Yin was credited with helping arrange Newsom's 2023 trip to China according to a story co-authored by his organization in New York-based Taiwanese newspaper the World Journal.

The newspaper article said that C.C. Yin began negotiating the visit "after being entrusted by the governor's office" to "formally [convey] Governor Newsom's desire to visit China to Consul General Zhang Jianmin."

His brother Henry Yin accompanied the governor as an adviser on the October 2023 visit, where Newsom met Chinese President Xi Jinping, the Journal reported.

Henry Yin has also beenphotographed with Newsom at APAPA events, which he shared on Facebook.

Newsom's spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. The governor is among those expected to seek the 2028 Democratic nomination for president.

Henry Yin also acted as an adviser to California congressman Ro Khanna, who is similarly talked about as a potential Democratic 2028 presidential candidate and is currently the ranking member of the House Select Committee on the CCP, established with the purpose of monitoring Chinese government influence in U.S. politics. Henry Yin and C.C. Yin have personally donated $15,800 to Khanna's congressional campaigns since 2017.

Khanna's spokesperson has since given statements about Henry Yin's relationship with the influential lawmaker that conflict with Khanna's own social media posts.

A 2019 Facebook post by Khanna included a photo of Henry Yin presenting the congressman with a birthday cake, with the caption announcing that "Henry will serve as my Senior Advisor on Foreign Trade and Economic Development." In a 2020 post he referred to Henry Yin as a "good friend."

Until this month, Yin listed on his LinkedIn page a current role as "Sr. Advisor to US House of Rep [Ro] Khanna," beginning in 2019. The page has since been deleted.

Khanna appeared alongside Henry in February this year at a Sunnyvale, California event run by APAPA-affiliated PAC, Asian Americans for Good Government. Both Henry Yin and C.C. Yin have been listed as board members of the PAC, according to archives of its website.

Earlier this month, his spokesperson told the New York Post that Henry Yin "has never held a formal role with the Congressman." In a subsequent statement to CBS News, Khanna's communications director Sarah Drory said that Henry Yin "served for a year as one of dozens of volunteer leaders."

Drory added in the statement that "APAPA has been a decades-long organization to empower Asian Americans and it's an ugly anti-Asian smear to suggest ties" to the Chinese government.

news.title: JD Vance Chances Against Ossoff, Buttigieg and AOC: Latest 2028 Polls
news.text: With the 2028 presidential election more than two years away, Vice President JD Vance is trailing four potential Democratic rivals in early general election polling and carries a narrow lead over one. A polling average tracked by the analytics account Race to the WH shows former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Democratic Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff leading Vance in hypothetical general election matchups. Buttigieg leads Vance 48.5 percent to 43.9 percent, while Ossoff has a similar lead, 48.5 percent to 44.1 percent. Ossoff has repeatedly said he has no interest in running for president in 2028. Former Vice President Kamala Harris also leads Vance, 48.3 percent to 44.4 percent, while Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom holds a narrower lead, 45.5 percent to 43.6 percent. Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is the only Democrat in the average who trails Vance, at 42 percent compared with Vance's 44.9 percent. No candidate in either party has formally entered the 2028 race. The tracker lists Buttigieg, Ossoff, Ocasio-Cortez, Harris and Newsom among its most-polled Democratic names. On the Republican side, Vance has said he will wait until after November's midterm elections to discuss his own plans. Buttigieg Runs Strongest Against Vance Buttigieg holds the widest lead of any Democrat tested against Vance in the Emerson survey behind the Race to the WH averages and the former transportation secretary is gaining ground. Eight percent of voters were undecided in that matchup. Buttigieg was also the only Democrat in the poll with an identical five-point lead in a hypothetical matchup against Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the Florida Republican often viewed alongside Vance as a potential top 2028 contender. Ossoff and Newsom saw their leads over Rubio narrow to three points and two points, respectively, while Harris trailed Rubio by five points despite leading Vance. A year earlier, the picture looked different. Emerson's July 2025 poll had Vance ahead of Buttigieg by a single point, 44 percent to 43 percent, with 13 percent undecided. "A key takeaway from the ballot tests is that about 13% of the electorate remains persuadable, while the other 87% have already settled on a party preference," Spencer Kimball, Emerson's executive director, said at the time. Buttigieg's numbers track with his standing in a hypothetical Democratic primary. Emerson showed him leading the field with 19 percent in July, and Quantus Insights put him at 25.7 percent in August, ahead of Ossoff at 21.3 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 15.3 percent. A Saint Anselm College Survey Center poll in New Hampshire showed him at 25 percent, again the highest of any potential candidate. Ossoff Matches Buttigieg's Margin Ossoff has nearly the same lead over Vance as Buttigieg, and he leads Rubio by three points as well. His national profile has grown this year, after getting little attention from major pollsters last year. Ossoff has seen strong numbers in recent polling. An August Quantus Insights survey had him at 21.3 percent among Democrats, third behind Buttigieg and ahead of Ocasio-Cortez. But he led all named candidates among voters who described themselves as only leaning Democratic, at 33.5 percent. Prediction markets also see the Georgia senator—who is currently running for another term in the Senate—as a competitive name in the Democratic field, with Ossoff at 17 percent on Kalshi, followed by Ocasio-Cortez at 16 percent and Newsom at 14 percent. Polymarket has him at 17 percent, just behind Ocasio-Cortez at 18 percent. Vance Leads Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez is the only Democrat among those tested who trails Vance in the current average, and she was the only candidate in Emerson's August survey to lose to both Vance and Rubio. Removing undecided voters from the Quantus poll narrows the gap to 51.9 percent for Vance and 48.1 percent for Ocasio-Cortez. The Quantus crosstabs show a familiar coalition split. Ocasio-Cortez led among women, 48.7 percent to 37.1 percent, and voters aged 18 to 29, 53.4 percent to 24.9 percent. Vance led among men, 53.9 percent to 34.4 percent; among voters 65 and older by a similar margin, and among voters without a college degree, 52.9 percent to 36 percent. Ocasio-Cortez led among Black, Hispanic and Asian respondents, while Vance led among white voters. She also led among urban voters, 53.6 percent to 32.6 percent. The one survey showing Ocasio-Cortez ahead came months earlier. A December poll from The Argument and Verasight had her leading Vance 51 percent to 49 percent. She posted the result on X with a single word: "Bloop!" Asked about the poll by reporters, she said, "Let the record show: I would stomp him. I would stomp him!" How the Numbers Have Moved Looking back at Emerson's numbers from 13 months earlier, there are notable changes. Buttigieg gained six points on Vance, while Newsom gained eight. Ocasio-Cortez gained one point, a change small enough to fall within the margin of error in both surveys. Undecided voters fell from 13 percent to 15 percent in July 2025 to 7 percent to 8 percent in August 2026, with the shift favoring Democrats rather than splitting evenly. Ossoff was not included in the ballot test a year ago. Vance's position among Republican primary voters also changed over the same period. He had 52 percent support in Emerson's February poll, but that fell to 36 percent by May, when Rubio was at 35 percent. Two months later, Vance led Rubio 39 percent to 38 percent. Emerson pollster Spencer Kimball described the race as having shifted "significantly" toward Rubio. Vance has not offered a timeline on decisions about his future beyond the midterms. "Usha and I will absolutely sit down and talk about what comes next for our family," the vice president told CBS Sunday Morning in June, adding that he expects President Donald Trump to be "very supportive" of whatever he decides. Rubio, who has moved closer to Vance in the Republican primary polling, has said he does not intend to challenge him. "If JD Vance runs for president, he's going to be our nominee, and I'll be one of the first people to support him," Rubio told Vanity Fair back in January. Trump has continued to draw comparisons between the two, at one point calling a potential Vance-Rubio ticket "unstoppable" without saying who would lead it. He later told reporters that "JD is fantastic, and Marco is fantastic." The broader political environment has also shifted during the period. Democrats have led the generic congressional ballot by seven to 11 points in Emerson's surveys since the spring, while Trump's approval rating has remained in the high 30s to low 40s. What Prediction Markets Say While JD Vance's odds of winning the Republican nomination are strong according to Kalshi and Polymarket, with him leading Rubio on both platforms, his odds of becoming the next White House occupant trail well behind in the 2028 winner market, with Kalshi rating it at 22 percent to 23 percent and Polymarket rating it at 20.7 percent to 20.8 percent. Both numbers have fallen since the markets opened. When Polymarket launched its 2028 book in July 2025, Vance was priced at 56 percent for the Republican nomination and 27 percent to win the White House. He has since given up roughly five to six points in each race, ground that has mostly gone to Rubio, whose nomination odds have more than tripled on both platforms. That number is part of a broader market view that already favors Democrats in the 2028 presidential race. Kalshi has Democrats at 60 percent to Republicans at 40 percent, while Polymarket has Democrats at 67 percent to Republicans at 34 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: Vance is trailing Ossoff and Buttigieg in early general election polling while holding a narrow lead over Ocasio-Cortez.

news.title: Kamala Harris steps up midterm campaigning as 2028 ambitions remain in focus
news.text:
ReutersKamala Harris is increasing her campaign appearances for Democrats while considering a presidential run. Her visits to Michigan, Nevada, and Georgia are strategically important for the party.

Former US Vice President Kamala Harris is stepping up her campaign appearances for fellow Democrats as she considers whether to make another bid for the White House, beginning with a visit to Michigan on Tuesday to support Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.The trip marks a significant return to a state where Harris suffered a defeat to President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. Michigan is also among six states set to launch the Democratic Party’s next presidential nominating process.Also Read: New York 17: Can Mike Lawler hold a district Kamala Harris won?Harris has further campaign appearances planned in Nevada and Georgia, two states that are expected to remain important to the Democratic Party’s electoral strategy. Her increased involvement in the midterm elections could help shape perceptions of her prospects for a future presidential campaign, while also exposing her to renewed scrutiny from Democrats who want the party to move beyond its 2024 defeat.“I think she's run her course,” said Barry Goodman, a Democratic National Committee member from Michigan who raised money for both Joe Biden and Harris. “I just don't think her running again would be the right thing for America moving forward.”Live EventsSome Democratic candidates have already distanced themselves from the prospect of campaigning alongside Harris, particularly in states that Trump won by wide margins. Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico, “No thanks. Let's move on. We need some new leadership.”Others, including influential Black women who supported Biden’s decision to select Harris as his running mate in 2020, have argued that she should be allowed to consider her political future without pressure to make an immediate decision.California Governor Gavin Newsom recently told CNN that he would not seek the Democratic presidential nomination if Harris decided to run.“Kamala isn't under any deadline to run for anything,” said Donna Brazile, a former Democratic National Committee chair who managed Al Gore’s 2000 presidential campaign. Brazile described efforts to revisit Harris’s shortened 2024 campaign as a “waste of time” and said potential presidential contenders “should follow Kamala's lead and get out there” to support candidates in the midterm elections.Harris has not announced any upcoming visits to South Carolina, where Democrats are scheduled to hold their first primary. Antjuan Seawright, a political consultant in the state, said Harris could make a case for herself but would need to demonstrate that a future campaign would be different from her previous one.“She's going to have to admit that she was wrong about some things,” Seawright said.Michigan offers Harris both risk and opportunityMichigan carries particular significance for Harris because of the political fallout from the 2024 election. Arab American communities in the state strongly criticised the Biden administration’s support for Israel’s military operations in Gaza and were disappointed that Harris did not break with Biden after becoming the Democratic presidential nominee.Also Read: Harris tells Dems to fight back, stop waiting for 'Republican epiphany' ahead of US midterm pollsEl-Sayed, meanwhile, has been an outspoken critic of Israel and has described the war in Gaza as a genocide against Palestinians, a characterisation rejected by Israel. His views have raised concerns among some Jewish voters, and he has sought to address the controversy by apologising for certain past comments.“There were some hurt feelings” in Michigan following the 2024 election, El-Sayed told MSNOW, adding that some Black voters believed Arab Americans had not done enough to support Harris.He described Harris’s visit as an opportunity “to bring communities together that have often been torn apart by recent events.”The appearance will also draw attention to the political differences between the two Democrats. Harris has had a strained relationship with the party’s progressive wing, while El-Sayed is seeking to strengthen establishment support in his contest against Republican nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman.“We can build together on the areas of agreement, and we can come to understand each other far better on the areas where we might have seen eye to eye, and I think her coming into town will help us to do that,” El-Sayed said.Harris’s campaign travel has been limited compared with that of other potential 2028 contenders, including Pete Buttigieg, who ran for president in 2020 and later served as Biden’s transportation secretary. Buttigieg recently visited South Carolina and has been campaigning for Democratic candidates in the midterms.Harris visited South Carolina in the spring for smaller local party events. She has also participated in an organising call focused on registering and mobilising an additional 1 million Black voters.“There's value in doing a lot of stuff behind the scenes instead of being front and centre, especially for her,” said Bre Maxwell, a Democratic National Committee member from South Carolina. Maxwell said Harris had little incentive to place herself at the centre of news cycles while remaining “a target of Donald Trump right now.”Jaime Harrison, a South Carolina Democrat who served as the national party chair during Biden and Harris’s time in the White House, said Harris’s prominence gave her more time than other potential candidates to decide whether to run.“Many of these folks who do get in quickly would love to have that type of name ID, would love to have that type of network, to have that type of email list,” Harrison said.Harris has repeatedly said she is in no hurry to decide her next political move. In a recent podcast appearance, she said, “Right now - midterms, midterms, midterms.” Her spokesman, Eduardo Negron, declined to comment on her timeline.Her other campaign appearances this autumn include events supporting Nevada Democratic gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking reelection and has himself been mentioned in discussions about the 2028 presidential race.“She is certainly being strategic,” Seawright said.He noted that Harris’s tour for her campaign memoir, *107 Days*, took her to nearly every major Southern city in states where Black voters have a significant influence on early Democratic primary contests.Goodman said he had heard no evidence that Harris was actively working the Democratic Party’s top donor network. Harrison said he had not spoken to her since December.Lessons from previous campaignsHarris first sought the Democratic presidential nomination during the 2020 election cycle, when she was a US senator from California. She withdrew from the race in late 2019, before any primary votes were cast.Her record as a former prosecutor drew criticism from some progressives, who viewed her as part of a criminal justice system that disproportionately imprisons Black men. Some moderates, meanwhile, regarded her as a liberal politician from San Francisco.Biden later selected Harris as his running mate, making her the first woman and first Black person to serve as US vice president.After Biden ended his reelection campaign following a poor debate performance, Harris became the Democratic nominee and initially generated strong enthusiasm. She drew large crowds, delivered a speech at the party’s national convention and received favourable reviews for her debate performance against Trump.However, she struggled to distinguish herself from Biden on issues including inflation and immigration. During an appearance on *The View*, Harris said she could not think of anything she would have done differently from Biden. Trump also targeted her support for transgender rights in campaign advertisements, declaring, “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”Seawright said Harris would need to adopt a clearer approach if she ran again, including a willingness to reconsider some of her earlier positions.“She's going to have to admit that she was wrong about some things,” he said, adding that voters “reward that kind of authenticity and humility.”Harrison said Harris would have greater scope to develop her own political agenda outside the constraints of the vice presidency. But he also cautioned that she would need to move beyond the formalities and protections associated with the office.“You can't act like a sitting vice president, standing up on that stage,” Harrison said. “I'd tell her she has to run hard, just as hard as everybody else, working every rope line, taking every selfie.”Unlike Biden’s decision to hand the nomination to Harris in 2024, Harrison said, the next Democratic presidential contest would be “the wild, wild west.”Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Democratic Rep. Jared Golden Endorses Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in Key Race
news.text:
Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) endorsed Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) on Sept. 21, crossing the aisle to support the Republican in one of the most closely watched House races of the midterm cycle.

In an op-ed published in The Journal News in White Plains, New York, Golden, who is not seeking reelection, pointed to his work with Lawler on legislation protecting Maine’s lobster industry. He also cited Lawler’s support for Democratic efforts on federal workers’ union rights and health insurance subsidies.

“Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent,” Golden wrote. “I strongly back him, and I hope voters send him back to work. Wherever you live, find the members who pass laws with the other party, and keep them. Maine’s lobstermen can tell you how much it matters.”

Lawler commented on the endorsement in a post on X.

“It’s an honor and a privilege to accept the endorsement of my friend, Democratic Congressman Jared Golden,” Lawler wrote. “While we are from different parties and different states, Jared and I have worked during our time together in the House to find common ground on issues that matter both to us and our constituents. We share a firm belief that what’s best for the people should come before one’s party, and that if more members on both sides of the aisle took that approach more often, the country would be better off for it.”

Lawler faces Cait Conley, a Democrat and an Army veteran who won her party’s June 23 primary, in New York’s 17th Congressional District. Lawler has represented the Hudson Valley district since 2023 and is one of three House Republicans whose districts then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried in 2024.

The Epoch Times reached out to Conley’s campaign and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee for comment on the endorsement. Neither responded by publication time.

Golden built much of his case around the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act, which he introduced with Lawler this year. The bill would extend a pause on new federal right whale regulations affecting the lobster industry from 2028 to 2035. It passed the House 219–196 on Sept. 1 and now goes to the Senate.

“It is worth knowing who is leading that bill with me: Rep. Mike Lawler, a Republican from New York’s Hudson Valley. There is not a single lobster boat in his district. He got no votes in this and no headlines back home,” Golden wrote. “He signed on because a historic American industry, thousands of fishing families, and the principle that federal rules should be built on facts were all on the line.”

Golden said that Lawler also signed on to his bill restoring collective bargaining rights for federal employees after the Trump administration made changes. He also said Lawler signed a Democratic discharge petition to force a House vote on extending the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits.

“Lobster traps, union rights and health insurance do not have much in common, except that on all three, Lawler chose to solve the problem rather than campaign on it,” Golden wrote.

Golden, a Marine Corps veteran who has represented Maine’s 2nd Congressional District since 2019, announced in November 2025 that he would not seek a fifth term. He criticized candidates who cast fellow Americans as the country’s biggest threat, without naming any.

“We have real adversaries in this world, and they are not our fellow citizens. When candidates for office tell voters that the gravest danger to this country is other Americans and the leaders they elect, that is radical talk, and it is the same politics of fear I have refused to practice for my entire career,” Golden wrote.
news.summary: The retiring Maine Democrat cited Lawler's bipartisan work with him on lobster regulations, federal workers' union rights, and health insurance subsidies.

news.title: GOP Rep. Mike Lawler picks up shock endorsement from retiring House Democrat Jared Golden
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Democratic Rep. Jared Golden bucked party lines Monday and urged New Yorkers to back Hudson Valley Rep. Mike Lawler for re-election in an ultra-competitive race that could determine the balance of power in the House.

Golden (D-Maine), who announced last year he would not seek another term in Congress — and is no stranger to defying party bosses — praised Lawler (R-NY) as a “true partner” in the often-divided legislature.

“[T]he country needs fewer members who treat the job as a stage and more who treat it as work,” Golden wrote in an op-ed for The Journal News. “In New York’s Hudson Valley this fall, that is the choice on the ballot.”

“Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent. I strongly back him,” the Democrat went on. “Wherever you live, find the members who pass laws with the other party, and keep them.”

Golden, 44, was referencing Lawler’s assistance on the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act, which the House approved earlier this month. 

That bill delays until 2035 the implementation of new fishing regulations meant to protect whales. Golden had warned that some 18,000 fishing jobs in his home state would be affected if the new rules went into effect.

The day after his bill passed, Golden defied House Democratic leadership and voted for a GOP procedural motion, known as a “rule,” that helped Republicans get that week’s agenda through the chamber.

Typically, rule votes in the House occur on a party-line basis, but Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) prevented Republicans from having to send the House home early on their pre-midterm recess.

“I held the most challenging district of any Democrat in the country [Maine’s Second District] by earning the trust of Democrats, independents, and Republicans alike,” Golden wrote. “Lawler holds one of just three Republican seats in the country that Kamala Harris carried in 2024.”

“Representing districts like ours forces you to work for people who disagree with you, and it teaches you that those people are not your enemies. They are your neighbors.”

Lawler also hasn’t been afraid to defy GOP leadership, having clashed with President Trump last year to secure a larger hike to the state and local tax (SALT) deduction cap in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act than what was initially proposed.

Polls indicate Lawler is running neck and neck against Democrat Cait Conley in New York’s 17th District.

Conley’s campaign for comment did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
