news.title: Golden breaks Democratic ranks to support Lawler’s reelection bid
news.text:
New York Republican Mike Lawler, one of the most vulnerable members of the House, picked up a notable endorsement Monday from retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine.

In an op-ed for The Journal News, Golden pointed to the pair’s work on several bills, including one that would extend a pause on federal lobster regulations until 2035, noting that Lawler signed on to the measure despite it not affecting his Hudson Valley district. 

“He signed on because a historic American industry, thousands of fishing families, and the principle that federal rules should be built on facts were all on the line,” Golden wrote. “And he understands that in every community, not just in Maine, mom-and-pop shops have been around for generations, and their livelihoods make up the very foundation of our communities.”

“Mike Lawler has been a true partner to me and a friend to fishing families he will never represent,” he added. “I strongly back him, and I hope voters send him back to work.”

Golden announced last year that he wouldn’t seek reelection to Maine’s 2nd District, a largely rural seat that President Donald Trump has carried all three times he’s been on the ballot, including by 9 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales. 

Lawler, in contrast, is among a handful of House Republicans who represent districts that backed Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Harris carried New York’s 17th District by less than a point, while Lawler was reelected by 6 points. 

Lawler currently faces a tough fight for a third term against Democrat Cait Conley, an Army veteran who also worked for the National Security Council and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency during the Biden administration. Inside Elections rates the race a Toss-up.

Lawler said it was “an honor and a privilege” to receive Golden’s support. 

“We share a firm belief that what’s best for the people should come before one’s party, and that if more members on both sides of the aisle took that approach more often, the country would be better off for it,” he posted on social media Monday. 

Over his tenure in the House, Lawler has sought to build a reputation as a moderate who will work across the aisle, while not shying away from his party label.

Lawler spoke earlier this month at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, an event that some swing district Republicans opted not to attend. Speaking onstage, he said his remarks were directed at “common sense Democrats and independents” who were “concerned about the rise of socialism and extremism on the left” and not sold on Republicans either. 

“The president and I don’t always agree, and that’s OK,” said Lawler, who joined Trump at a campaign rally in Rockland County earlier this year. “But in contrast to what the media tells you, what I learned about President Trump behind closed doors is that if you're willing to make your case and fight for what you believe in, he's willing to listen.”

Golden, meanwhile, has twice this month drawn the ire of Democratic leaders by joining with House Republicans on procedural votes that would have fallen short without support from him and Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Pérez, who represents a battleground seat in Washington state. 

One of those votes was on a rule governing debate on four bills, including the lobster measure Golden worked on with Lawler, and a resolution to denounce “socialism in all its forms.” The other vote helped advance several items, including legislation to impose new sanctions on Russia.

news.title: Republicans Are Losing Key Supporters That Fueled Donald Trump's 2024 Win
news.text: Gen Z voters powered President Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 election. But, two years later, Republicans are losing ground among the youngest voting group amid economic anxiety, according to several recent polls published ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Key Takeaways Why It Matters Trump’s inroads with Gen Z voters were among the most surprising developments of the 2024 election. Young voters historically vote for Democrats by wide margins, but Trump lost them by only 11 points to former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, 54 percent to 43 percent, while winning young men by a single point, according to CNN exit polling data. That’s a historically strong showing for a Republican in modern politics. However, the latest polls have found Gen Z voters shifting leftward for the midterms, another warning sign for Republicans in the battle for control of both the House of Representatives and Senate on November 3. Gen Z also held gloomy views toward the economy, a major driver of voter behavior in those surveys. The president’s party historically loses congressional seats when he is unpopular, and Trump’s national polling numbers have fallen across all voter groups since his 2024 campaign, when he emphasized affordability as a cornerstone of his election bid. Americans continue to face high prices, and economic concerns including tariffs, the high cost of living as well as surging gas prices amid the unpopular war with Iran have contributed to the decline in Trump’s popularity. Democrats Winning Over Gen Z Voters Gen Z voters are backing Democrats by large margins ahead of the midterms, the latest polls of the generic ballot show. In a poll from The New York Times, Democrats were winning over those between the ages of 18 to 29 by 35 points, 64 percent to 29 percent, with 7 percent saying they are not sure who they would vote for. That represents Democrats’ strongest voting bloc by generation. They won those 30 to 44 by 21 points, 57 percent to 36 percent. Republicans won those 45 to 64 by 2 points, 49 percent to 47 percent, while Democrats won those 65 or older by 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. Overall, Democrats led the generic ballot by 8 points, 51 percent to 43 percent. The poll surveyed 1,503 voters from September 8 to 13, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Democrats were also winning Gen Z in a new Fox News poll. Among those under 30, Democrats had a 29-point lead, 63 percent to 34 percent. It surveyed 1,211 registered voters from September 11 to 14, 2026. Similar numbers were reported by YouGov, which gave Democrats a 21-point lead on the generic ballot, 51 percent to 30 percent, with 12 percent undecided and 6 percent saying they would not vote in the midterms. It surveyed 1,461 registered voters from September 11 to 14, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. Nina Raneses, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, told Newsweek that young people "deserve leaders who are fighting for them." "Trump has failed to deliver on his promises to young people, instead raising prices, worsening corruption, and deepening American involvement in foreign conflicts. This November, the contrast couldn’t be more clear: while Trump and Republicans have betrayed young Americans, Democrats are lowering costs and creating a brighter vision for their futures," Raneses said. Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek that Republicans are "making it easier to buy a home and more affordable to start a family." "Meanwhile, Democrats are pitching a fantasy—that everything can be free—and it's the same empty promise as a kid running for student body president on 'more recess for everyone.' Families deserve real answers, not fluffy campaign slogans," she said. Donald Trump Approval Rating Among Gen Z Negative views toward Trump could be a major factor shaping Gen Z’s voting behavior in the midterms. In the poll from the Times, only 18 percent of respondents between the ages of 18 and 29 said they approve of Trump’s job performance. The Fox News poll found that only 29 percent of those younger than 30 approved of him. That number was 31 percent in the YouGov poll. That’s lower than the general population in each of those polls. His overall approval rating stood at 38 percent in the poll from the Times, 39 percent in the Fox News poll and 40 percent in the YouGov poll. Gen Z Economy Views Young Americans are not optimistic about the state of the economy, the polls have found. In the poll from the Times, only 9 percent rated the economy as being either good or excellent, lower than any age group. The Fox News poll found that 68 percent of those younger than 30 believe Trump’s policies have made the economy worse, compared to 42 percent who are older than 45 and 62 percent 65 or older. The YouGov poll, however, told a different story. It found that 32 percent of those 18 to 29 described the economy as being excellent or good, a stronger number than other age groups. How the Youth Vote Has Shifted Over the Years Trump receiving 43 percent of the vote among those ages 18 to 29 marked a high point for him compared to 2020 and 2016, when he received 36 percent of the vote in each election. Republicans also struggled with the youth vote in 2008 and 2012, when former President Barack Obama won the group by large margins. The last time they backed Democrats by a single-digit margin was 2004, when John Kerry won them by only 9 points, according to exit polling data from The New York Times. What Happens Next Polls will continue to be closely watched over the coming weeks ahead of the midterms as a key gauge to how all voters are responding to ongoing political developments. Candidates are making their cases to voters and facing off in debates as November 3 inches closer. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and James Debens

news.text:
As Kamala Harris considers whether to seek the presidency once again, she is immersing herself in the midterms by campaigning alongside fellow Democrats, beginning with a Tuesday trip to Michigan on behalf of Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

The stop is a particularly significant choice for the former vice president. Michigan was among seven battleground states she lost to Donald Trump two years ago, and it now stands as one of six states that will initiate the next presidential nominating process for Democrats. Harris also has upcoming rallies set for Nevada and Georgia, two other vital stops on the political landscape.

Her campaign appearances could either solidify or weaken her standing as a prospective Democratic front-runner. Although she remains one of the nation's most recognizable politicians and a pathbreaking figure, others in the party are eager for a fresh chapter after she failed to defeat Trump when she replaced President Joe Biden at the top of the ticket.

"I think she’s run her course," said Barry Goodman, a Michigan Democratic National Committee member who raised funds for Biden and later Harris. "I just don’t think her running again would be the right thing for America moving forward."

A number of Democratic candidates, particularly in regions Donald Trump carried easily, have flatly rejected the prospect of appearing with Harris. "No thanks," Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico. "Let’s move on. We need some new leadership."

Yet many Democrats, including influential Black women who helped persuade Biden to choose Harris as his running mate in 2020, contend she has earned the right to deliberate over her options without being pushed aside or criticized. Emphasizing her distinct position, California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently told CNN he would not enter the contest if Harris runs.

"Kamala isn’t under any deadline to run for anything," said Donna Brazile, a former Democratic National Committee chair who managed Al Gore’s 2000 presidential bid. Calling it a "waste of time" to dwell on Harris’s shortened 2024 campaign, she suggested other White House contenders "should follow Kamala’s lead and get out there" to assist midterm candidates.

Harris has not announced visits to South Carolina, where Democrats will hold their opening primary. Antjuan Seawright, a political consultant based there, said she could present a compelling case, though a future campaign would need to look and sound different.

"She’s going to have to admit that she was wrong about some things," he said.

Harris shares a complicated history in the state, where prominent Arab American communities grew angry over Biden's support for Israeli military actions in Gaza and were disappointed when Harris did not separate her stance from his after becoming the nominee.

El-Sayed, by contrast, is a prominent critic of Israel who has called the war a genocide against Palestinians, a description Israel rejects. He has faced concern from some Jewish voters, which he has tried to navigate by apologizing for past controversial statements.

El-Sayed noted to MSNOW that "there were some hurt feelings" in Michigan following the 2024 election, with some Black voters feeling Arab Americans did not offer enough support to Harris.

With the former vice president visiting, he sees an opportunity "to bring communities together that have often been torn apart by recent events."

The joint appearance will draw intense focus for other reasons as well. Harris maintains a complicated relationship with the party's progressive wing, which includes El-Sayed, while El-Sayed aims to secure establishment backing in his contest against Republican nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman.

"We can build together on the areas of agreement, and we can come to understand each other far better on the areas where we might have seen eye to eye, and I think her coming into town will help us to do that," El-Sayed said.

Harris' travel schedule remains light compared to other prospective candidates like Pete Buttigieg, who ran in 2020 before serving as Biden’s transportation secretary. Buttigieg recently visited South Carolina and has been actively campaigning for midterm Democrats.

Harris visited South Carolina in the spring for smaller party functions, and recently joined an organizing call aimed at registering and mobilizing 1 million Black voters.

"There’s value in doing a lot of stuff behind the scenes instead of being front and center, especially for her," said Bre Maxwell, a Democratic National Committee member from South Carolina. She noted little reason for Harris to step into media cycles knowing "she’s still a target of Donald Trump right now."

Jaime Harrison, a South Carolinian who served as national party chair under the Biden-Harris administration, said her standing gives her a timing advantage other potential candidates lack.

"Many of these folks who do get in quickly would love to have that type of name ID, would love to have that type of network, to have that type of email list," Harrison said.

Harris has stated repeatedly, including in an Associated Press interview last year, that she feels no pressure to decide her plans. "Right now – midterms, midterms, midterms," she told Megan Rapinoe on a recent podcast. Spokesman Eduardo Negrón declined to comment regarding her timeline.

Her other upcoming campaign appearances include events for Nevada’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Aaron Ford, and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is sparking 2028 speculation of his own while running for reelection.

"She is certainly being strategic," said Seawright, the South Carolina consultant.

He pointed out that her book tour for her campaign memoir, "107 Days," visited nearly every major Southern city in states where Black voters carry heavy influence in early primary contests.

Meanwhile, Goodman said he sees no sign that Harris is engaging top party donors, and Harrison noted he has not spoken with her since last December.

Harris first ran for president in the 2020 cycle as a U.S. senator from California, but exited in late 2019 before any votes were cast.

Some progressives viewed the former prosecutor as part of a system that disproportionately imprisons Black men, while some moderates saw her as a typical San Francisco liberal.

Biden selected her as his running mate, making her the first woman and Black person to serve as vice president.

When Biden ended his reelection effort after a poor debate performance, Harris energized voters, generating crowds matching or exceeding Trump’s. Her convention address and debate performance drew praise from many analysts.

However, she struggled to distance herself from Biden on inflation and immigration, famously telling interviewers on "The View" she could not think of anything she would have done differently. Trump targeted her in advertisements focusing on her support for transgender rights, declaring: "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you."

If she runs again, Seawright said she must stress moderate positions and "be willing to say, you know, ‘I’ve rethought some things.’" Voters, he added, "reward that kind of authenticity and humility."

Harrison observed that presenting her own platform would be easier than when "she was a sitting vice president, somebody else’s No. 2." But he warned she must shed the formal trappings of the vice presidency.

"You can’t act like a sitting vice president, standing up on that stage," he said. "I’d tell her she has to run hard, just as hard as everybody else, working every rope line, taking every selfie."

Unlike 2024, Harrison warned, "This is going to be the wild, wild west."

news.title: Trump Goon’s Dictionary Comeback Blows Up in Her Face
news.text:
A White House spokesperson’s attempt to cite the dictionary to “prove” that Donald Trump’s immigration policy isn’t racist has spectacularly backfired on her. 

The U.S. State Department last year created a secretive “Office of Remigration” that was apparently inspired by Europe’s extremist movements seeking to expel people for simply being foreign. 

But the Trump administration has been desperate to argue with its critics over the word’s meaning, saying that it does not mean forcibly expelling people from the country. 

A new report in The Washington Post details how senior State Department officials originally objected to adopting the term “remigration” because of its roots in white supremacism.

They showed the acting remigration head a Wikipedia article that detailed the word’s racist origins, but during an all-hands call on June 9, 2025, the new Office of Remigration was announced.

Career officials continued to push back on the office, which seemed to promote “ethnic cleansing via the mass deportation or promoted voluntary return of non-white immigrants,” according to one staffer. 

Trump officials, however, insisted it was the exact terminology they wanted. 

Asked by the Post about the white supremacist associations, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement: “Not everything you dislike is racist. Remigrate literally means to migrate back. By returning illegal aliens to their origin country, we are simply enforcing our nation’s laws.” 

Bis also included a link to the Merriam-Webster Dictionary definition of “remigration,” though the entry didn’t have the intended effect. 

As the Post pointed out, one of the definitions listed is “the forcible return of immigrants and often their descendants to the immigrants’ countries of origin.” 

The White House has repeatedly denied remigration’s European extremist roots, while at the same time using white nationalist rhetoric and imagery to discuss Western values and Western civilization, NPR reported in December.

During his 2024 presidential campaign against former Vice President Kamala Harris, Trump vowed in a Truth Social post to “end the migrant invasion of America,” and to “revoke deportation immunity, suspend refugee resettlement, and return Kamala’s illegal migrants to their home countries (also known as remigration).”

When a former Afghan special forces soldier opened fire on two National Guard members last November, the president used the deadly shooting as an excuse to attack immigrants and announce his plans to “permanently pause migration from all Third World Countries” to “allow the U.S. system to fully recover” from a supposed influx of “illegal and disruptive populations.”

“Only REVERSE MIGRATION can fully cure this situation,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post in the days following the shooting. “Other than that, HAPPY THANKSGIVING TO ALL, except those that hate, steal, murder, and destroy everything that America stands for—You won’t be here for long!”

The White House previously defended the policy in a statement to the Daily Beast, saying: “President Trump was elected as the president of the United States based on the many promises he made to the American people, including his promise to deport criminal illegal aliens. He is keeping his promise to the American people.”

But the Office of Remigration’s activities go far beyond deporting migrants to their countries of origin, according to the Post. 

Trump’s remigration chief, Christian Ehrhardt, has negotiated at least $410 million worth of agreements with 31 African and Latin American countries to accept deportees who have no connection to the host country. 

The 41-year-old career State Department official, who previously worked in embassy protection, is technically a deputy assistant secretary of state, but he negotiates the so-called third-country deportation deals as a “White House envoy” sent by deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the Post reported. 

The resulting contracts are meant to bypass statutory requirements—including human rights protections—that govern most foreign assistance spending, with some agreements involving countries ruled by authoritarian regimes, sources told the paper.
news.summary:
Win McNamee / Getty ImagesA White House spokesperson’s attempt to cite the dictionary to “prove” that Donald Trump’s immigration policy isn’t racist has spectacularly backfired on her. 

The U.S. State Department last year created a secretive “Office of Remigration” that was apparently inspired by Europe’s extremist movements seeking to expel people for simply being foreign. 

The president has also repeatedly called for “remigration” or “reverse migration,” a previously fringe concept that has gained widespread attention in Europe thanks to a former neo-Nazi political activist from Austria. 

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: John Oliver Roasts MAGA Nepo Baby Gunning to Be His New Boss
news.text:
John Oliver has torn into the MAGA nepo baby whose rampage across the media industry could soon swallow up the comedian’s show. 

The late-night comic veered off course from another segment to discuss 43-year-old Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison.

The British comic noted that Mangione has amassed an online following among those who also take a dim view of UnitedHealthcare’s history of denying life-saving care. Oliver cited the example of a woman whose parents were forced to pay for her cancer treatment.

“Now, in the end, her parents paid $95,000 out of pocket to cover the treatment, which in happy news did actually work, but having access to wealthy parents just cannot be the system to get badly needed healthcare—even if it is apparently the system that lets you be in charge of HBO,” he said, pulling up a picture of Ellison.

Ellison, whose father is tech billionaire and Republican megadonor Larry Ellison, is gunning to take over HBO, which airs Oliver’s show, after his firm Paramount Skydance reached a $110 billion sale agreement with the network’s parent company, Warner Bros. The elder Ellison is putting up $40.4 billion to backstop that deal.

“Yeah, my soon-to-be business daddy has a literal business daddy,” Oliver went on. “And to be very clear: I deeply respect that and I would never make fun of you for it, unlike that pesky Stephen Colbert.”

That last remark was a nod to just some of the controversy surrounding the younger Ellison’s merger of his firm, Skydance, with Paramount last year. 

The merger went through only after Paramount paid $16 million to settle a lawsuit brought by Donald Trump alleging that one of its news networks, CBS, had deceptively edited an interview with his former Democratic opponent Kamala Harris to give her an edge in the 2024 polls. 

Colbert, whose program, The Late Show, was aired on CBS, called that payment a “big fat bribe,” given the merger had relied on approval from the Federal Communications Commission, which Paramount Skydance subsequently secured. 

CBS promptly announced a “purely financial decision” to cancel Colbert’s show. The network has since undergone a conservative programming overhaul, notably at CBS News under new editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. 

The Daily Beast has contacted Paramount Skydance for comment on this story.

HBO/Last Week TonightJohn Oliver has torn into the MAGA nepo baby whose rampage across the media industry could soon swallow up the comedian’s show. 

The late-night comic veered off course from another segment to discuss 43-year-old Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison.

Oliver was talking about UnitedHealthcare’s record of failing desperate customers on Sunday’s edition of Last Week Tonight ahead of the sentencing in December of Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty in court last month to killing the group’s CEO Brian Thompson.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Trump asked Republicans to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot.’ But his ask is based on a myth.
news.text:
After driving North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis into retirement, Trump visited the state on Wednesday to campaign for GOP nominee Michael Whatley, who is trailing Democrat Roy Cooper in the polls.

“I’m asking you to just pretend I’m on the ballot just one more time,” the president told the crowd. Trump has made this request of GOP voters repeatedly in recent weeks, including at last week’s midterm convention in Texas.

But there’s a problem: When Trump was on the ballot in 2024, he did not help swing-state Republicans down that ballot.

In many states, thousands of Trump voters went to the ballot box, pulled the proverbial or literal lever for him and left without voting for other Republicans.

In 2024, Trump won all seven swing states: Pennsylvania, Georgia, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin, Michigan and Nevada. Of those seven, all but two (Georgia and North Carolina) had Senate races. And of those five, the GOP won one: Pennsylvania, by about 15,000 votes out of close to 7 million. As for the House, Republicans lost two seats.

This was not just due to split-ticket voting. In many states, thousands of Trump voters went to the ballot box, pulled the proverbial or literal lever for him and left without voting for other Republicans.

And that’s before we factor in an aging former President Joe Biden, who had a disastrous public debate and quit the race. After that decision, unprecedented in American history, Vice President Kamala Harris struggled to define herself and her campaign on short notice. From immigration to crime to inflation, not one issue was in favor of the incumbent Democratic Party. All of this was historic, and historically bad for Democrats.

In that political atmosphere, the shock of 2024 was not that Trump won, but how little he won by. Had results swung one point toward Harris in Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, she would be called “Madame President.” And Trump could not carry fellow Republicans to a wider victory in a year that simply could not have been worse for Democrats.

The pendulum continues to swing in American politics, and it blindsides politicians who deny what Americans see every day. 

Now in 2026, after saying he’d lower prices, they’re even higher. He took the country into a war of choice with Iran, which is divisive even among the MAGA base. An end to the conflict, let alone victory, is proving elusive. Republicans previously cited high gas prices as putting incredible stress on working people and American families. On Election Day 2024, the average price of gas was $3.10 per gallon. As of Friday, it is $4.47 — and rising.

Meanwhile, Trump has traded stocks by the thousands and pursued a myriad of vanity projects, from arches and ballrooms to fountains and helipads. Even Trump’s signature issue of immigration enforcement, once his strongest in polling, is now poisonous with the public due to the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s aggressive behavior. Today Trump’s average approval rating is in the mid to high 30s, and headed down. The winning collation of 2024, with its gains among independents, the young and Black and Hispanic voters, is crumbling.

In place of a legislative agenda, the president has even tried to promise Americans a $5,000 “dividend.” Even if this pledge weren’t as mythical as his other promised checks, this inflationary approach to affordability is like trying to treat emphysema with a carton of Marlboros.

The pendulum continues to swing in American politics, and it blindsides politicians who deny what Americans see every day. We are a bitterly divided nation and anything is possible in the midterms. But if Trump could not help swing state Republicans in 2024, it is incredibly hard to think 2026 will somehow be better for the president and his party.

news.title: Does James Talarico Have a Chance?
news.text:
In 2018 a captivating congressman from El Paso nearly turned Texas blue. In a race against Sen. Ted Cruz that captivated Democrats nationwide, Beto O’Rourke lost by a modest 2.6 points, the closest a Democrat has come to winning a Senate or governor’s race in Texas in modern memory.

Although this performance was still a loss that earned Democrats exactly zero Senate seats, it augured a bright future for Democrats in the state. “Blue Texas,” foretold since the Obama era, seemed on track. That perception grew in 2020, when Joe Biden lost the state to Donald Trump by only 6 points in a presidential year, improving 3 points on Hillary Clinton’s loss in 2016. The state’s color was turning.

And then, in 2024, Texas Democrats, as O’Rourke told me, “got what they deserved.”

Kamala Harris lost the state by a whopping 14 points. While the country shifted rightward as a whole, the turn against Democrats among Latino voters turbocharged the collapse in Texas. Cruz easily won another term in the Senate. “Blue Texas” had never seemed further away.

Which makes it all the stranger that only two years later, we’re doing this again. Because Democrat James Talarico really could win a Texas Senate race.

The political-media industrial complex has been down this road before. No one—no reporter, operative, commentator, analyst, or person on the street—wants to look like an idiot by overhyping it again. I certainly don’t. But after weeks of speaking with politicians and experienced campaign hands in Texas, there’s no denying it: There’s more to this race than the usual hopium.

“You’d have to work pretty hard to not recognize that this is different,” University of Texas professor James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project, told me. “That this Senate race is different than any Senate race we’ve seen for a couple of generations, let alone any statewide race.” He noted that in the run-up to the 2018 Texas Senate race, O’Rourke never led in any polls. Meanwhile, Talarico has led or tied in all but one recent poll.

“I think Talarico is just one of, if not the, best candidates we’ve ever seen,” O’Rourke himself told me.

Democrats have not won a statewide race in Texas since 1994. Especially given their setback in 2024, it was clear going into 2026 that Democrats would need a perfect storm to win. They just might get it.

The national environment is at Democrats’ backs. Talarico is a compelling and well-funded candidate—albeit one not without baggage—running against a scandal-plagued and poorly funded opponent in Attorney General Ken Paxton. The strong gains Trump made among Latinos in South Texas over the issues of cost of living and immigration are reversing over the issues of … cost of living and immigration. There’s a populist revolt over data centers and Flock cameras. Gas is expensive. Everyone is mad.

But it’s not just the conditions. There’s something more fundamentally different this time in Democrats’ approach. What struck me as I was talking to Democrats about this cycle is that, unlike in previous runs that had their hopes up, they’re not relying on vibes to do their work for them. The past failures and overhyping has chastened them and offered much to learn from, and they may well be learning it: They’re not promising a new era of Democratic Party rule in Texas. They’re just focused on winning this race, this time, and not squandering the opportunity that has fallen into their laps.

Democrats’ future—not just in terms of winning control of the Senate in 2026, but in terms of staying competitive with Republicans in the long run—depends on their learning to win in red states. Have they finally cracked the code?

Why does the idea of Texas turning blue hold such fascination in Democrats’ hearts? Why don’t charismatic Democratic candidates from Mississippi or Tennessee make the cover of Vanity Fair, rake in record amounts of money, and capture Democrats’ national attention?

It’s not just because Texas is the crown jewel of red America, the second-largest state in the country with the second-biggest allotment of electoral votes. It’s because, unlike many other comfortably red states, there was a period when its demographics were shifting in a way that aligned with those of the Democratic Party. During the Obama years, the state was becoming younger, more concentrated around metropolitan areas, more diverse, and more white-collar. This was the coalition that Democrats were betting on for transformative change across the country, the party’s then recipe for an enduring majority.

The idea, then, was not that Texas Republicans were going to convert en masse to voting for Democrats. It was that their majority would be diluted away as Democrats registered more and more Latino voters, assured to be on their side. College-educated transplants would flood to the orbits of Austin, Houston, and Dallas. Suburban voters would veer away from the GOP.

The appropriate way to interpret this information was, and is, that Democrats had the ability to make Texas a competitive state. The inappropriate way to handle it was, and is, to think that assumed demographic change guaranteed that Texas would inevitably turn blue and it was only a question of when. This latter stance can breed an idleness that, as we’ve now seen, ensures it may not happen at all.

One of the first tests of this era of demographic promise was the 2014 governor’s race, when Greg Abbott ran for election against Democratic state Sen. Wendy Davis.

Davis had gone viral in 2013 for a 13-hour filibuster against a state legislative bill restricting abortion. She had a compelling biography, as someone raised by a single mother who rose to graduate from Harvard Law School. Helping her along in the field was Battleground Texas, an organizing group founded in 2013 by former Obama aides with the goal of registering Democratic-leaning voters in the state. While Battleground tried to explain that it was playing a long game, its linkup with Davis, who was attracting extraordinary national attention, applied pressure on both to show immediate results. But it was an awful election year for Democrats nationally, and Abbott defeated Davis by 21 points.

“That was partly our fault,” Davis told me in an interview of the way expectations got out of hand. “Because when you’re running a campaign, you do need to build belief that it’s going to be different this time.”

She didn’t have as forgiving a stance for the group that helped her along: “The unfortunate thing is there were a lot of big promises and hopes made by Battleground in that cycle,” she added, “that, when they didn’t come to fruition, some of the folks leading that effort just moved on.”

Perhaps given that hangover, the O’Rourke campaign started off with low expectations in the 2018 cycle.

“The O’Rourke campaign was not at first built to win,” Jeff Rotkoff, a Texas Democratic strategist who directed campaigns for the Texas AFL-CIO in 2018, told me. “In fact, they were dismissive of efforts of others to help them win.” Indeed, they were dismissive of Rotkoff’s own efforts to help them: He described to me how O’Rourke initially missed out on the AFL-CIO’s endorsement because his campaign hadn’t asked for it. The whole operation had a general “too cool for school” attitude early in the campaign, Rotkoff said, in which it rejected opportunities to work with the rest of the party infrastructure.

But then it grew into a proper movement—not just among liberals nationally, but in Texas as well. And yet, to some degree, O’Rourke’s campaign was still winging it. Texas Democrats I’ve spoken to over the years have a way of framing O’Rourke’s 2018 Senate run as not only a highly impressive achievement … but also something they’re comfortable Monday-morning quarterbacking. There’s a pervasive sense that maybe he could have won if he’d just done a few things differently—though what those things are is up for debate.

Part of the problem, everyone seems to agree, is that the party infrastructure itself wasn’t prepared for a competitive statewide race. The gubernatorial candidate, Lupe Valdez, “was sort of a sacrificial lamb” in the governor’s race against Abbott, as Henson put it. And the primary focus of the national Democratic Party was on flipping several suburban House seats, not on driving O’Rourke across the finish line.

Rotkoff wanted to be clear that these weren’t attacks on O’Rourke personally, and that “they learned a lot of lessons” in real time. The point of comparison, though, is with the Talarico campaign, where “the strategic political analysis was there from the start.”

“It’s not just a vibes deal,” he said.

This time, as former Texas Democratic Party Executive Director Manny Garcia told me, Talarico “doesn’t bear the burden of having to do it by himself.”

Democrats have recruited a candidate for every state and federal race on the ballot, no matter how doomed the contest, to ensure that persuadable voters everywhere are hearing the message. (Republicans have derided this move as a gimmick.) The state party is cooperating with the Texas Majority PAC—in other words, with George Soros’ dollars—to provide resources. And Democrats have landed a strong gubernatorial recruit in state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, who sits next to Talarico in the state Capitol, to both challenge Abbott in a difficult year—making him work unusually hard for his fourth term—and reinforce the message of corruption the two candidates are using against their opponents.

Talarico is “bringing so much interest to Texas, lots of money to Texas, and it helps me and my appeal to certain constituents. So we are complementing each other in a way that is very helpful for the statewide ticket,” Hinojosa told me in an interview. “There is this synergy happening up and down the ballot that we have never had before in Texas, and I do think that is a difference-maker.”

So Democrats have the candidate. They have the environment. They have the opponent. They have the ticket. They have the money. They even have the strategy.

Do they have the voters?

One is hard-pressed to find a more dramatic shift in voter behavior between 2016 and 2024 than that of Latino voters in Texas.

Hillary Clinton, per exit polls, won this cohort 61 percent to 34 percent in 2016. Eight years later—and with Donald Trump remaining precisely the same person he was, saying the same things he’s always said, every day, over the course of that stretch—Trump won 55 percent of Latinos in the state. Results on county-by-county levels are jaw-dropping. As the Washington Post reported after the 2024 election, 13 of the top 15 counties in the country with the largest rightward swings between 2016 and 2024 were in Texas. They’re all majority Hispanic.

What happened? Everything.

Inflation and economic hardship, which led to fond remembrances of the Trump economy from 2017 to 2019. Chaos at the border. Working-class Latinos joining the broader working-class turn away from the Democratic Party. Voters being another generation removed from their newness to the country and attaining a more conservative socioeconomic status. Social conservatives responding to leftward shifts among Democrats on cultural issues. Name something, and the answer is probably yes.

This helps explain Democrats’ losses, from Davis to O’Rourke to Harris: The party may have gotten the demographic shifts it was expecting, but it never translated into the political coalition it predicted. As James Henson put it to me, “The growth of the Latino population relative to the Anglo white population was going to be a lot more complicated than the demographical-destiny trope really took into account.”

And just about every Democrat and Republican I spoke to for this story said that Democrats took these voters, particularly in the Rio Grande Valley, for granted—“based on the color of their skin or their country of origin,” as Beto O’Rourke put it.

A better way to put it, though, is that Democrats never had these voters secured in their coalition the way they thought they did.

“Latinos felt for a long time like Democrats were the lesser of two evils,” Sergio García-Rios, an assistant professor at UT and director of polling for Univision, told me, “but that Democrats never deliver.” Democrats “thought, for a long time, that the only thing that mattered was immigration, to Latinos, and immigration reform.” But immigration reform never materialized, anyway. And then, after the parade of inflationary and border-security maladies under Biden, it was time to give something else a shot.

“There’s a lot of people who are working class in these areas who voted Democrat for a long time, and their life hasn’t gotten any better,” Chuck Rocha, a veteran Democratic strategist—who is advising both Talarico and Hinojosa this year—told me.

“And then along comes Donald Trump, who sounds a lot like, if you close your eyes, Bernie Sanders,” Rocha added. “He’s talking about a rigged system. He’s talking about remanufacturing jobs in America. That’s kind of how Donald Trump controlled that space while Democrats don’t spend any money juxtaposing that position, because there’s no real party infrastructure in McAllen or in Brownsville.

“And that’s the perfect storm,” he concluded, “that put us in a position where not all of those people automatically came on board like their mothers and grandmothers.”

In the long run, Democrats’ ability to win back Latino working-class voters will hinge on their ability to win back working-class voters more broadly. But as far as 2026 goes, the upside for Democrats with Latino voters’ swingy voting preferences is that they can swing right back from Republicans’ 2024 highs. And they can even do so largely on the same issues with which Trump won those voters: the cost of living, and immigration.

Manny Garcia, formerly of the Texas Democratic Party, told me that “people wanted something in economic terms that was being promised” by Trump. He added: “And right now, what people are seeing is, ‘Well, my prices aren’t going down like you promised, I’m not having a better economic outlook like you promised, and I am getting consistently disrespected. My family’s getting consistently disrespected. My community’s getting consistently disrespected.’ ”

On immigration, Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and former campaign manager for John Cornyn, noted that Latinos in South Texas “want a secure border, don’t want the cartels to run rampant, we don’t like human trafficking, we don’t want to see immigrants dying in the desert of thirst.” At the same time, though, the current Trump administration has gone well beyond what they find acceptable. Now they also realize they “don’t want these excesses, don’t want the federal government to come in and round up everyone, especially people that don’t have a criminal past.”

As Steinhauser put it: “There’s not a lot of support among Hispanic Texans in South Texas for doing mass deportation of people who are not violent criminals.”

The polling shows clear signs of a reversion, with polls of Latinos in Texas backing down hard from Trump’s 2024 margins while Talarico enjoys strong support among them in his race against Paxton. A recent survey from Univision and YouGov showed Talarico leading among Latinos 56 percent to 37 percent.

This flip is worth understanding specifically. Because it’s not that all of the voters Trump picked up in 2024 suddenly, in the words of Rocha, are “going to run up and become democratic socialists or start dyeing their hair blue or get a nose ring.” It just means that some of those who felt that promises made to them were broken could sit this election out.

“Not all of those guys are coming back, and they still think that Democrats are queers or weak,” he added. “But they’re really pissed at Republicans.”

As much as this is Texas Democrats’ best opportunity in modern memory to win a prestigious statewide race, it is, ultimately, only that: an opportunity. And James Talarico is a long way from winning this race.

Talarico has been ahead in polls over the summer, with strong support from independents, but he’s rarely polling above 50 percent. The great question is whether Texas Republicans will come home for their candidate, warts and all.

Their candidate has behaved confusingly. Ken Paxton has been running an anti-campaign at times so baffling that it’s worth considering whether his ability to get others to do his work for him is actually genius.

To quote his felled primary opponent, Sen. John Cornyn, “Paxton’s a poor campaigner” who’s “lazy and doesn’t raise money. And he basically is not offering a very compelling case for his election.” As of the latest filing deadline, which covers the first two quarters of the year, Paxton had only $16.7 million (with joint fundraising committee hauls factored in), while Talarico had raised $72 million. Paxton was literally on vacation in London, famously the home of the British monarchy, with his girlfriend on America’s 250th anniversary. When he does bother to campaign, he makes peculiar choices, such as at a late August event for which he wore a Four Seasons Orlando–branded golf shirt and what appeared to be a $40,000 watch.

All this, of course, is layered atop his history of having been impeached by the state House, having faced an untold number of corruption allegations, and having been divorced by his wife on “biblical grounds.” That he’s made it this far is because he’d remained in Trump’s favor after trying to overturn the 2020 election through a lawsuit hastily dismissed by the Supreme Court.

What Paxton must have known, though, is that once he became the nominee, he’d be golden. National Republicans can’t afford to lose his race—outside money would have to swarm to prop him up. And, sure enough, the cavalry has finally arrived. After a lengthy finger-pointing match between Trump, Senate Republicans, and Texas donors about who was responsible for rescuing Paxton, they’re all chipping in. Between the recent commitments from Trump’s super PAC, Senate Republican leaders’ super PAC, and others—including Elon Musk—Paxton managed to close the spending gap with Talarico in a week.

That money will allow Republicans to amplify Talarico’s most prominent weakness: his history of getting carried away during what is now called “Woke 1.0.” In 2020 and 2021, Talarico said that “God is non-binary,” that there are six biological sexes, and that “white skin gives me and every white American immunity from the virus” of racism. More recently, CNN uncovered an appearance by Talarico in a 2020 Sierra Club forum in which he said that he was “thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country,” describing them as “oppressive systems” in need of “dismantling.”

Talarico has tried to dismiss old comments like these as “cringey.” But with the right ad budget behind them, they could be just cringey enough to send Republican-inclined voters, noses held firmly, to pull the lever for Paxton.

Then again, it’s quite something to see nearly $100 million in super PAC money dumped into Texas, in September of an election year, to save a Republican Senate candidate.

The GOP’s late attempted rescue of Ken Paxton coincided with the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in early September, and Paxton’s role in this showcase was largely to serve as the butt of a joke. He himself gave lackadaisical remarks on the convention’s first night—alongside everything else, Paxton is also an unenthusiastic public speaker—to an indifferent crowd. For the rest of the convention, he was subjected to Trump’s regular insults about how he dresses poorly and looks bad. Paxton, waiting for his super PAC money to arrive, just stood there and took it.

If Texas Democrats can’t beat this guy, in this environment, could they ever have a chance in Texas?

It’s a question for Democrats in states across the country this year.

Each red state in which Democrats are competitive in 2026 is a little different. Ohio and Iowa are less diverse but have more recent Democratic DNA in them, having voted for Barack Obama twice. Right now they’re being hit hard by Trump’s trade (and real) wars. Alaska is uniquely reliant on the federal government and has a large independent streak. What Texas, Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio all have in common is the national wind at their backs, strong candidates, and decisions by Trump that went out of their way to make life in their states more difficult. They also all prompt a lot of heartburn about races over the past decade that fell short despite initial signs of promise and alluring polling numbers the September before the election.

Should Democrats get swept in all these races, under these dreamlike conditions, Democrats nationally may, once again, forswear ever getting emotionally or financially invested in these states. (Or at least for another two years, when they find themselves inevitably tempted again.)

The issue is that soon, converting red states where Democrats have lost their foothold—not just fantasizing about converting them—will become a necessity for the party.

Republicans already have a structural advantage in the Senate with their strength in small, rural states, giving Democrats limited options and narrow paths toward a Senate majority. And after the 2030 census, Democrats are going to need some fresh electoral votes. States like California and New York are projected to lose multiple congressional districts, while various other blue states will likely lose individual seats. This gives Democrats fewer Electoral College options and will officially retire the old “Blue Wall” pathway to victory of winning Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin (not that this pathway has been the most reliable recently). That means Democrats will need more options to win a presidential race. And there’s no better place to make it up—and beyond—in one fell swoop than Texas, to where many of those blue-state congressional districts will be transferred after the census.

“We damn sure better be investing in Texas now than in 2032,” Wendy Davis told me.

In other words, the long-term dream of “blue Texas” from the Obama years, seen as a way to lock in an inevitable, prolonged Democratic era, could soon become the medium-term need for “blue Texas” just for Democrats to keep up.

The first order of business, though? Well, you’ve just got to win a race.
news.summary: Democrats for decades have been seeing a “blue Texas” on the horizon. They have paid for it dearly. But they’re trying something new this time.
news.author: Jim Newell

news.title: US Election ‘Nostradamus’ Allan Lichtman Is Back With 10 New Keys
news.text: Allan Lichtman has outlined a new 10-point framework for assessing presidential greatness ahead of the release of his upcoming book on transformative American leaders. The political analyst built his public reputation through the Keys to the White House, a system designed to forecast presidential elections. Lichtman is often dubbed the "Nostradamus" of presidential politics because his model correctly predicted the winner of most U.S. presidential races for decades, making him one of the country's most closely watched election forecasters. His record came under renewed scrutiny, however, after he incorrectly predicted that Vice President Kamala Harris would win the 2024 presidential election, a race ultimately won by President Donald Trump. His newest project turns away from prediction and instead asks a different question: what makes a president historically great? The framework serves as the foundation of Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, out September 22, which identifies a dozen presidents whom Lichtman believes fundamentally altered the country's trajectory. From Predicting Elections to Measuring Greatness Lichtman told Newsweek that his new model is centered on consequence rather than popularity. According to the historian, the 10 keys measure the extent to which presidents seized the defining challenges of their eras and changed the nation's course. Public approval, contemporary polling and ideological agreement are not part of the calculation. "The clearest illustration is that I included James K. Polk and excluded Dwight Eisenhower," Lichtman said. "Eisenhower was a fine president who outranks Polk in nearly every expert survey. But Polk doubled the size of continental America, and Eisenhower changed the country far less. If the framework measured esteem, that result would be indefensible. It measures consequence, so it follows." What Are the 10 New Keys? The 10 keys include crisis leadership, transformational change, moral vision, stewardship of executive power, coalition building, institution building, diplomatic influence and adaptability. More specifically, the categories are: How the Framework Handles Presidential Failures Transformative leadership alone is not enough to qualify as great, Lichtman argues. He says candidates for inclusion must operate within the broad traditions of American democracy. That principle helps explain why Richard Nixon and Donald Trump are excluded despite their undeniable influence on national politics. A central role is played by what Lichtman calls the Stewardship Key, which evaluates whether presidents "expanded executive authority responsibly" rather than through what he describes as "reckless overreach." Newsweek reached out to the White House via email for comment on Sunday. For presidents who make the list, major failures are considered alongside major achievements. Lichtman cited Lyndon B. Johnson as an example, saying the Vietnam War is weighed against domestic reforms that he ranks among the most consequential in modern American history. A System Built for Debate Lichtman acknowledges that different historians could apply the same keys and still reach different conclusions. Rather than presenting the framework as a mathematical formula, he describes it as a structured guide requiring human judgment. Its purpose, he says, is to encourage debate while forcing evaluators to identify the specific criteria behind their assessments. "The keys are gauges, not an algorithm," Lichtman told Newsweek. "They require judgment at every turn, like every system dealing with human behavior. I make no pretense that mine is the only defensible set of judgments." Under that approach, historians might disagree over how heavily to weigh transformational change or whether a president satisfies the Moral Vision Key. What matters, Lichtman argues, is that disagreements become focused on concrete historical questions rather than instinctive rankings. He has previously described the model as a "do-it-yourself" system for evaluating presidential greatness and says its educational value lies in encouraging discussion about American history. Why No Modern President Makes the Cut One of the book's most striking conclusions is that no president after Ronald Reagan presently qualifies as great. Lichtman offers several explanations. First, historical distance matters. Assessing a president's true impact becomes more difficult when the long-term consequences of their decisions have not yet fully emerged. He also points to structural changes in American politics. In his view, growing partisan polarization accelerated after the 1994 midterm elections, when Republicans gained control of both chambers of Congress for the first time in four decades. As ideological overlap between the parties diminished, consensus became increasingly difficult to achieve. Social media, he argues, intensified those divisions by creating information silos and enabling highly targeted political messaging. At the same time, presidents now face a more demanding governing environment. Challenges range from geopolitical competition and terrorism to cyber threats, globalization and climate-related issues, all while managing a vastly larger federal government. Lichtman states that recent presidents have generally functioned as capable managers rather than transformational leaders. While figures such as George W. Bush, Bill Clinton and Barack Obama experienced periods of success, he contends they did not fundamentally overcome the deeper forces driving national division. What 2024 Taught Him About Political Models Lichtman draws a sharp distinction between his new framework and the Keys to the White House. Election forecasting, he says, involves predictions that can be proven right or wrong by future events. The presidential greatness model, by contrast, is retrospective and evaluative. Still, the 2024 election prompted him to consider whether some of the historical assumptions behind his forecasting model are becoming less reliable. His election system is based on the idea that voters act primarily as judges of the incumbent party's governing performance. Lichtman says one question raised by 2024 is whether "polarization" and "an unprecedented avalanche of misinformation" have weakened that relationship. He remains unconvinced that the underlying premise has collapsed. Yet he argues the possibility deserves serious attention, particularly because it connects to a broader theme running through the book: that the conditions which once produced transformative presidents may be eroding alongside the political environment that allowed voters to evaluate them clearly. As a result, the 10 Keys to Presidential Greatness are not merely a ranking tool. They are also an argument about how American leadership has changed and what it now takes for a president to leave a lasting mark on the nation. Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation by Allan J. Lichtman is set to be released on September 22, 2026. news.title: Republicans are unleashing their fundraising advantage against the Democrats
news.text:
WASHINGTON—Republicans are pumping money into a series of Senate and House battleground states, unleashing one of their biggest advantages over Democrats as they seek to overcome electoral headwinds in the final weeks before midterm elections.

Democratic candidates have mostly outpaced their Republican opponents in fundraising, but the GOP has maintained a significant lead among their network of super PACs and party committees—and are beginning to open the spending spigot in significant ways.

Advertisers supporting Republicans across 10 key Senate races have spent more than $204 million in the first 18 days of September, according to AdImpact—$83 million more than those helping Democrats. It is a sharp turn upward from all of August, when the Republican spending advantage was about $9 million.

The onslaught could help Republicans level the playing field as they seek to overcome President Trump’s unpopularity and voter discontent with economic malaise and climbing fuel prices.

View full Image

“I think we’re going to have enough money. I think if we have a bad result in the midterms, I don’t think we’ll be able to blame it on money,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R., La.), who has traveled extensively in support of GOP candidates, including planned stops this weekend in Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska.

“You’ve got both sides basically saying the other side’s worse than me, and it’s hard to win an election like that. Thank God, I’m sorry for the country, but politically, thank God that the Hamas wing of the Democratic Party is in control. Otherwise, we’d be total lunch meat,” Kennedy said.

Democrats hope that an expanded map of races into once-safe Republican districts will put Trump and his allies on the defensive and force difficult spending decisions in the final weeks, negating some of their fundraising advantage.

“The hole that Donald Trump has dug for the Republicans and continues to dig every day is not something that can be made up with a few $100 million worth of feel-good ads,” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.), saying that “people are angry” about the economy, the Iran war and corruption.

The most dramatic uptick came in Texas, with $62 million in ads supporting Republican Ken Paxton so far this month compared with about $17 million behind Democratic candidate James Talarico. Republican-supported spending this month exceeded that for Democrats in every Senate race considered a tossup by the Cook Political Report, the first time that has happened in this election cycle.

View full Image
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico at a campaign rally last month in Kerrville, Texas.

In House elections, Republican-aligned spending this month is ahead of Democrats in 15 of 21 races that Cook rates as a tossup, according to AdImpact. Spending in September, when most party primaries have completed, serves as a good early indicator of how the two parties may fare in head-to-head activity for the general election.

Earlier this month, the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc. disclosed spending $10 million on streaming TV ads to back Paxton and oppose Talarico, its first multimillion-dollar spend of the election cycle. On Saturday, it reported spending $5 million more. The group currently has less than $1 million in ads booked through the election, according to AdImpact, but other GOP-aligned groups are readying large spends. They include $169 million reserved by the Senate Leadership Fund, $155 million by the Congressional Leadership Fund, and multimillion planned spending from two new super PACs aligned with MAGA Inc., No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC.

Senate Republicans have urged their colleagues to make a robust pitch on steps the administration and party have taken to address inflation. During a Senate luncheon last week, Sen. Susan Collins (R., Maine), spoke of the need to pitch voters on economic prescriptions beyond tax cuts, including permitting reform for affordable housing and energy projects.

In Georgia and North Carolina, races considered leaning toward Democrats, ad-spending margins are tighter, and activity ramped up in August. Since then, spending supporting Sen. Jon Ossoff (D., Ga.) totaled $35 million compared with $26 million for his GOP opponent, Rep. Mike Collins. In North Carolina, ad spending favoring former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley totals $33 million since August, ahead of $25 million for former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat.

Republicans had sought to make defeating Ossoff a top priority, but he has vastly outraised Collins, and polls show him with a comfortable lead in the battleground state. In North Carolina, Cooper has held a steady advantage against Whatley.

If Republicans continue to trail in both of those races, it might mean the party will need to divert resources into other, more pressing states, including GOP-leaning Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall faces an upstart challenge from Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, a minister; in Ohio, where GOP Sen. Jon Husted is attempting to fend off former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat; and in Alaska, where Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces a formidable challenge in former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

More than $78 million has been spent since August in Ohio supporting Husted, AdImpact data shows, ahead of $57 million for Brown. And in Maine, backers of Collins have spent about $41 million since August, more than the $29 million for her Democratic challenger, former state Senate president Troy Jackson.

View full Image
Republican Sen. Susan Collins during a campaign stop last month in Kittery, Maine.

Collins’ defense remains a top priority for Republicans—the veteran senator is the lone GOP senator seeking re-election in a state carried by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Jackson only entered the race in August as a replacement for scandal-plagued Graham Platner, and has sought to catch-up quickly in fundraising.

“I’m not deterred by that. I mean, we’re going to be outspent,” Jackson said, pointing to an outpouring of volunteers to his campaign. “People in the state are upset.” Collins, meanwhile, has targeted Jackson’s voting history in the state legislature, including on taxes and spending. “I don’t know that there is a tax that Troy has seen that he hasn’t liked,” Collins told reporters earlier this month.

Senate Democrats in Washington also huddled last week with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan who hopes to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D., Mich.). Both Peters and Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D., Mich.) have pressed their colleagues to support El-Sayed’s campaign against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R., Mich.), who was narrowly defeated by Slotkin in 2024.

Michigan remains among the most competitive Senate races in the nation, and a sharp increase in advertising this month on the GOP side raised spending since August to about $39 million for Rogers versus $35 million for El-Sayed.

“Let’s all agree we have a broken and horrible Frankenstein of a campaign finance system, but when they’re swamping us with President Trump’s money, I’m going to rally other Democrats to try and gin up a response,” said Slotkin, whose 2024 Senate victory saw more than $200 million in the race.

In ad reservations, which can change, Republicans are scheduled to outspend their Senate opponents in several states, including in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Democrats have reserved more advertising time in Georgia, according to AdImpact.

Marc Short, a former Trump White House aide and adviser to former Vice President Mike Pence, said party fundraising is less important than it used to be because of the shifting media landscape. “There are so many other ways to get your message out,” Short said, adding: “Would you rather have the money than not? Yes. Is it a factor it used to be? No.”

news.title: Top expert warns GOP running out of time to save must-win midterm race
news.text:
Republicans are still running behind in a must-win swing state race in the coming midterms, and as one of the nation's top election forecasting experts warned, the party is almost out of time to turn things around.

As President Donald Trump's toxic reputation with voters has tanked the GOP's midterm prospects, it has grown increasingly possible that it might lose its Senate majority, as well as the House of Representatives. One of the make-or-break races in that fight is in Michigan, where former Republican congressman Mike Rogers has continued to trail his Democratic opponent, epidemiologist Abdul El-Sayed. Republicans have attempted to torpedo El-Sayed's chances by accentuating his progressive stances as too left-wing, as well as his past affiliations with controversial commentator Hasan Piker, but so far, these efforts have not seemed to seal the deal with voters.

Decision Desk HQ is an outlet considered to be one of the foremost sources for election results tracking in the U.S. On Sunday, its director of data science, Scott Tranter, told NewsNation that "time is running out" for Rogers to reverse his fortunes, adding that the race is "closer than it should be if you’re the Republicans and want to keep the Senate." Tranter's site currently gives El-Sayed a 67 percent chance of winning the race, with Rogers only having a 33 percent chance.

"El-Sayed’s got the momentum. It’s pretty undeniable,” Tranter explained. “Michigan’s going to start voting in about a month on the early side. And look, everything you know about Michigan –– about a third of that voing to come in before Election Day. So Mike Rogers’s time is running out.”

Tranter also agreed with host Chris Stirewalt that El-Sayed could face scrutiny from Michigan's notable bloc of pro-Palestinian Muslim voters, given his past support of former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose association with the Biden administration and its support of Israel was widely credited with tanking her chances in the state. He has also faced pushback from pro-Israel voters over his criticism of the country's war in Gaza and his support for ending U.S. military aid over the situation.

Rogers, meanwhile, has faced criticism for his transition over the years from a more traditional Republican to a staunchly pro-MAGA Trump loyalist. The former congressman has previously been supportive of the president's hugely unpopular tariff agenda, which has had an outsized effect on Michigan, especially with the recently reignited trade war against Canada. He has also been supportive of Trump's war in Iran, with The Nation describing him as a "mega-hawk who has pushed for war with Iran for more than 20 years."

news.title: Katie Miller concerned about legal bills if Democrats launch investigations into Trump inner circle
news.text:
The wife of top Trump administration official Stephen Miller says she fears looming legal bills if Democratic wins in the crucial midterm elections lead to congressional subpoenas for the president's inner circle.

”After the first Trump administration, my family spent money we did not have on lawyers because of multiple partisan Democrat led investigations into President Trump,” Katie Miller said Saturday on social media. “I watched as many of my friends also had no idea how to pay expensive legal bills because they simply served their country.”

She added: “You can’t convince me Democrats won’t do this again.”

Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, told Bloomberg Government in April that Stephen Miller was among several people the committee would subpoena if Democrats take control after the midterms.

Garcia also mentioned former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, her former associate Corey Lewandowski, FBI Director Kash Patel and now-Attorney General Todd Blanche.

“They would all be in front of us pretty consistently,” Garcia said at the time.

Katie Miller’s comments came in response to a Bloomberg podcast in which New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman put the likelihood of billionaire Elon Musk being subpoenaed at “100 percent.”

“People have privately told me that’s what they plan to do. I think that they will,” said Haberman, co-author of the best-selling book Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump.

Katie Miller served as an adviser to Trump's ad hoc, Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency before leaving the administration in May 2025 to work for Musk, whose estimated $946.5 billion net worth makes him the world's richest person.

Three months later, she told Axios that she'd left that job to launch a podcast for conservative women. It now has about 73,000 YouTube subscribers.

In April 2022, Stephen Miller — a two-term Trump aide who's now his deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser — testified by video for more than eight hours after receiving a subpoena from the Democrat-led House January 6 select committee.

He also testified in April 2023 before the federal grand jury that later indicted Trump for allegedly conspiring to prevent Congress from certifying his 2020 electoral loss to Joe Biden.

Special counsel Jack Smith dropped that case, and another in which Trump was accused of illegally hoarding classified documents after leaving the White House, following Trump's 2024 victory over Biden's vice president, Kamala Harris.

Katie Miller, who was an aide to Vice President Mike Pence during Trump’s administration, avoided having to testify about the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol by Trump supporters because she was on maternity leave at the time.

Republicans hold a narrow, 219-214 House majority with two vacancies, and the GOP also controls the Senate, 53-47.

Polls show Democrats leading in the so-called generic congressional race, 50.4 percent to 42.3 percent, according to Real Clear Polling, but the Cook Political Report rates future control of both chambers as a toss-up.
