news.title: PRedictions, PRojections, PRaise, and PRedators: From AM to AI, It’s a Manic Media Landscape
news.text:
Another tell I gleaned: If all the ads are targeting someone else, this show wasn’t created with me in mind. So, if I saw something interesting in TV Guide, turned on the show, and saw that all the ads were for Barbie dolls, makeup, and feminine products, I usually nope’d outta there.

Because ad executives aren’t (entirely) stupid. In the Before Time — that forgotten era when the Tech Gods couldn’t digitally surveil our every move — an ad executive’s job was aligning his ad buys with his product’s demo. The ROI was straightforward and testable: The smarter the ad buy, the more products were sold.

It unmasked a show’s real, actual audience.

That brings us to today’s cable news networks, including Fox News, CNN, MS NOW, and Newsmax. What kind of commercials are they showing?

Right: Reverse mortgages. Incontinence medication. Drugs for old people.

It’s not a healthy demo!

Same goes for AM radio. Between 2015 and 2025, we lost over 340 AM stations. Dozens more went off the air in the first half of 2026.

Radio’s economics have shifted: Budgets are birth-strangled. A yuuuge number of news-talk AM stations are now 100% syndicated feeds, plus a few local news reads.

There used to be multiple AM radio hosts in every city — morning, afternoon, and night. They became local celebrities. That model is vanishing, because today’s economics won’t allow it.

There’s less talent and fewer opportunities.

It parallels the painfully noticeable cable TV brain-drain: Once upon a time, landing a prime-time show on Fox News or CNN would make you a power player. It meant you were the best of the best; you had reached the pinnacle of your industry. 

Today, most of the top broadcasting talent is monetizing their wares on YouTube, independent media, or a subscription model. Fox News needs them more than they need Fox News. The days of media titans gatekeeping talent have ended.

The culprit? Competition.

We’re digitally wired 24/7. Cable TV and AM radio aren’t just competing against the other stations — they’re also battling Spotify, personal playlists, YouTube, X, Facebook, TikTok, audiobooks, and 3.7 million active podcasts.

I used to listen to radio all the time in my car. Couldn’t imagine traveling without it. Going from city to city, flicking through the dial, and discovering local hosts was almost a ritual.

Now, 99.9% of the time I’m listening to my music playlist (which rocks) or a podcast.

In PR, there’s a maxim: The medium is the message. That is is an overstatement, of course, but the theory behind it — that the medium shapes how the message is received — is true.

Radio and TV are different. (Just ask Richard Nixon in 1960.) TV and podcasts are different. (Just ask Kamala Harris in 2024.) In each example, the losing candidate focused their energies on old media — and was devoured by the new.

There’s a political advantage to staying ahead of the curve.

PRediction: It’s counterintuitive, but AM radio is still worth investing in — and will continue to be a political force.

Don’t get me wrong: It won’t be the mega-power it was during Rush Limbaugh’s heyday. Stations will continue to close, and budgets will continue to shrink.

Because digital competition isn’t going away. It’s still increasing.

But in an era of fear and doomerism, AM stations fulfill a public need that podcasts cannot. They’re the zig to the Internet’s zag.

During times of crisis, AM is there. When a storm knocks out power (and Wi-Fi), AM is there. When you’re driving down the highway and there’s a traffic or weather advisory, it’s usually updated on an AM radio station.

It’s a safety issue. AM radio is still the most cost-efficient way to broadcast news during emergencies.

There’s another reason, too: government shenanigans!

Just a few years earlier, AM was DOA.

The Hill (May 15, 2023): Say Goodbye to AM Radio: Why Carmakers Are Removing It From New Models

Your next car might be missing a button – the one to switch between AM and FM radio. Car manufacturers are increasingly opting to eliminate AM radio in their new vehicles.BMW, Mazda, Volvo, Volkswagen and Tesla, among others, have either already removed or plan to remove AM radio from at least some electric models. Ford is going even further, reports the Detroit Free Press, and ditching AM in all new cars – gas or electric.

Those plans are now on hold.

USA Today (Sept. 16, 2026): Bill to Require AM Radio in Automobiles Passes House

Members of the House of Representatives passed legislation to require AM broadcast radio devices in all automobiles on Tuesday, Sept. 15, a move to ensure than Americans have access to information during emergencies."Tens of millions of Americans tune into broadcast AM radio every day," House Energy & Commence Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie said on the House floor, according to a press release. "Farmers use AM radio for weather forecasts, local information, and crop reports, while older Americans rely on it for local news and programming."AM radio is a critical tool for emergency communications. When a disaster hits and a broadband network goes dark, AM radio can continue providing critical emergency information to communities," said Guthrie, a Kentucky representative.

PRojection: Most conservatives, I imagine, are of two minds on this. Generally speaking, we’re not crazy about government interference in private industry — or forcing manufacturers to include old technology that’s been dollar-voted obsolete. It isn’t exactly consistent with laissez-faire governance.

But on the other hand, AM stations are dominated by religious and conservative programming. They've had an enormous impact on political discourse. (Many of our VIPs are ex-Dittoheads — as am I.)

Bottom line?

Keeping AM in cars is good for the GOP.

Are the Republicans overplaying the safety angle to protect a favorable media platform? 

Sure. Politics is politics. (If the Democrats were in our shoes, they’d do the same thing.)

But that doesn’t mean the safety issue isn’t legitimate.

I thought this was interesting: On Reddit’s “Politics” message board — which is overwhelmingly left-wing and stridently anti-Trump — the comments were at least 75% pro-AM radio. Safety concerns were their go-to reason.

Which means that this will be an easy sell for the Republicans: Conservatives want to protect AM radio, and liberals fear their own shadow.

Play the safety card — and we’ll win the political benefit.

PRaise: To President Donald Trump for perfectly handling the next great media hysteria, AI and chatbots. His idea of an “AI Force” and an AI czar to mitigate AI doomerism was nothing short of genius.

Honestly? I don’t know what the AI Force is supposed to do. And neither does President Trump. (Or anyone else.)

Because it’s completely irrelevant — and that’s the point: An imaginary problem demanded an imaginary solution!

I’m not a doomer. I believe AI will be transformative, groundbreaking, and trigger vast socioeconomic changes — but these extinction-level pontifications are frickin’ goofy. Any technology with the power to help has the power to hurt, but the idea we’re creating AI deities that will conquer the planet within the decade is pessimistic, misanthropic hubris.

The inconvenient truth is that AI doomerism is the new environmentalism. It’s media hysteria over the next great media platform: AI.

So Trump answered their made-up concerns with a made-up job!

Y’know, sometimes I’m critical of President Trump — mostly because my expectations are so dang high — but I’m sure gonna miss him when he’s gone. Love the guy. His instincts are next-level.

When they made DJT, they broke the mold.

PRedators: Here’s a little media nugget that didn’t get much attention. And I’ll betcha a Diet Coke that Tucker Carlson won’t cover it.

Ars Technica (Sept. 18, 2026): FCC Lets Paramount Sell 49.5% Equity Stake to Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday approved Paramount Skydance’s plan to sell large equity stakes to the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar.Under US law, companies with licenses to run broadcast stations need FCC approval to have direct or indirect foreign ownership exceeding 25 percent of the company’s stock. Paramount says its indirect foreign ownership will reach 49.5 percent after it receives investments from the sovereign wealth funds and filed a petition asking the FCC to waive the foreign ownership limit.

The Sunni Muslim PR campaign is the biggest, most far-reaching campaign in world history. The amount of money that Qatar and Saudi Arabia have spent to sway U.S. public opinion is already in the hundreds of billions.

Meanwhile, left-wing celebrities like Mark Ruffalo have bitterly attacked the role of Jewish businessmen like Larry and David Ellison for their involvement in the Paramount merger. Ruffalo cited Israel as a contributing factor, too. 

Imagine what Ruffalo and Carlson would say if ISRAEL had purchased a 49.5% stake in Paramount! 

But because it’s Qatar and Saudi Arabia, it’s no big deal. Relax, guys. Nothin’ to see here.

That’s the media rule: No Jews, no news.

news.title: Raphael Warnock discusses Georgia's midterms, a 2028 White House run
news.text:
Sen. Raphael Warnock offered a blunt assessment of his party's 2026 hopes in Georgia this week and addressed whether he plans to run for the White House in 2028.

The lawmaker, who was elected alongside Sen. Jon Ossoff in 2020, praised his Democratic partner and friend in the Senate but issued a warning for those who believe that the Peach State is a sure bet for blue.

"I think the people of Georgia see the work he's doing and that's why you're seeing him show up in such a powerful way," Warnock told USA TODAY during Congressional Black Caucus week in Washington on Sept. 18. "That said, it's Georgia, it's a purple state. And these elections can go either way, and they can change very quickly."

Her Black dad couldn't go on a Capitol trip. She could be a US senator

Ossoff leads challenger Rep. Mike Collins in every poll released this general election cycle, but Georgia went for President Donald Trump in 2024 after Warnock and Ossoff helped flip the state with Joe Biden in 2020. Ossoff's viral hype has yielded widespread 2028 buzz as some voices within Georgia, including veteran journalist Greg Bluestein, have suggested that Warnock is the candidate best suited to run for the White House.

An NBC News poll released Sept. 20 found that Democrats are seen more negatively than Trump and the GOP, two years after former Vice President Kamala Harris lost the 2024 presidential race as voters split 29% positive to 50% negative.

Warnock said that he is focused on November's midterms, arguing that Democrats need to "put some guardrails" on Trump and hold him accountable as "the basis for anything that anybody might want to do in 2028."

"We have seen the most inept and unfit people be confirmed by the United States Senate to high cabinet posts with huge consequences for the people of Georgia," Warnock said, referring to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Warnock won a partial term in 2020 over Republican businesswoman Kelly Loeffler, who was later appointed by Trump to lead the U.S. Small Business Administration, in a special election to replace Sen. Johnny Isakson who resigned. Later, he prevailed over controversial NFL legend Herschel Walker for a full six-year term in 2022.

Warnock preaches at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s church

Warnock prevailed by nearly three points and is up for Senate re-election in 2028. As senior pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church, he still preaches in Atlanta at the longtime spiritual home of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

Throughout his time in public life, the two-term senator has infused faith into a broader argument for Democratic policies and priorities – now a national trend as liberal faith leaders run for office in highly competitive races across the nation.

James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, in Texas and Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor in Kansas, headline Democrats' field in traditionally red states with surprisingly competitive Senate contests.

To explain why he continues preaching, Warnock referred to a 1965 quote by King in which the civil rights icon reflected on his call to serve: "In the quiet recesses of my heart, I am fundamentally a clergyman, a Baptist preacher." Warnock said that King was "doing this public work, but it was guided by his values."

Warnock slammed his Republican colleagues for turning into "pretzels" to support Trump's agenda, calling out his Senate colleagues for supporting Kennedy and engaging in voter suppression.

"They're in love with power. Well, I'm in love with democracy. I'm in love with change," Warnock said. "And politics for me is just a set of tools, but my mission is change."

"Whatever office I decide to seek or not seek, it will be rooted in that fundamental sense of mission."

I want to take a look at this Fox News poll that just came out this week, showing that 62 percent of registered voters say that grocery prices are a major problem for their family. 61 percent say gas prices, housing costs, healthcare costs, clear majorities.

And the poll also showed that 63 percent in this Fox News poll, 63 percent of voters say that the Trump administration has made the economy worse.

SCALISE: Look, I share concerns about affordability. If you look at gas prices, we've been working to try to bring gas prices down. They are down from the peak that they were over $5 a gallon under Joe Biden. But they can be lower, and they will be lower, by the way, when Iran gets resolved.

You look at food prices. You know, we're working to bring food prices down. When President Trump took office, the big hype and hysteria was around the price of eggs. They were over $3 a dozen for eggs. Today, they're less than $2 a dozen because President Trump went to work on that.

There's a lot more work to do, Jonathan, but is the answer to look at what the Democrats' agenda is, which is trillions in new spending and increasing prices. Go look at the disparity on gas prices, by the way, Jonathan, between red states and blue states. Gas prices are $0.55 a gallon higher in blue states because a lot of their mandates and ridiculous things that they do to jack up the cost.

We're working to bring the cost down. We opened up more production so that we can produce our own energy in America. Joe Biden had shut that down. Democrats want to go back to those days, by the way, where we have to import our oil from foreign countries. That dramatically increases the cost.

So how are we going to bring costs down even more? Republicans clearly are working with the president to make life more affordable. Democrats want to go back to higher spending and higher costs in all of those areas.

KARL: I mean, gas prices are actually considerably higher now than they were when Biden left office. But I want to ask you, before you go, about another issue, about a Republican statewide candidate in Texas who posted on social media this picture of University of Texas students celebrating their big win last week.

And he said, how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners? This photo seems to have a lot of non-white students, many of them American citizens and University of Texas students. This was denounced by Karl Rove. He said he's going to be voting for a Democrat as a result of this, cannot support this guy. And Cornyn said something -- John Cornyn, the Republican Senator, said something very similar.

Is this the kind of message that Republicans need to denounce and make it clear you don't support this kind of stuff?

SCALISE: I denounce that. I don't know who he is, but I denounce that. If you look, we've denounced on both sides some of the things. You know, you don't see Democrats denouncing Hasan Piker and others who are advocating for some of the most radical anti-American views you can see. In fact, some of their candidates, their socialist candidates in this common sense versus crazy election this year, the Democrats want to take us to a socialist place where they're advocating for open borders again.

Defund the police is not just the opening bid. They want to go to defunding prisons now. So there is a sharp contrast in this election. We can easily denounce that. You don't see the Democrats denouncing a guy with a Nazi tattoo. You don't see the Democrats denouncing somebody who said, you know, America deserved 9/11 on the heels of the 25th anniversary. That's some of the crazy people that they want to be in charge in Washington.

And that's why I think you're going to see such a sharp contrast in this election, where people need to show up and vote, Jonathan.

KARL: All right.

SCALISE: This is an election where everybody needs to vote.

KARL: All right. Republican leader Steve Scalise, thank you very much for joining us this morning.

SCALISE: Thanks for having me. Appreciate it.

KARL: Coming up, a red state Republican senator says he's hitting the campaign trail. But you might be surprised to which states he is going to campaign. And he's actually surprised, too.

We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: I don't want them in my office. I don't them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can. And if they could straighten themselves out, you know, if they could straighten themselves out, I'd love it.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: All right. The Roundtable on the press ban and whether Republicans should be worried about losing in places where they have not lost in a long time.

We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

KARL: All right, the roundtable is here.

Former DNC Chair Donna Brazile, former Bernie Sanders campaign manager Faiz Shakir, political consultant and pollster Frank Luntz, and conservative talk radio host Erick Erickson.

Donna, let me ask you with this. This press ban, kicking these organizations out, why -- why do you think he is doing it, and why now?

DONNA BRAZILE, FORMER DNC CHAIR & ABC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: Well, first of all, the president's had a rocky relationship with the media since he came down those elevators in New York City.

He loves the media. He adores, you know, the back and forth. In fact, he tries to grow around the media when they're not treating him as well.

But I found it baffling that this week, right before the president of China makes his state visit to Washington, that the president would ban CNN, MS NOW and “Politico”.

Why now? There's no real reason. But I recall back in 1989 when the Chinese banned CNN from coverage.

KARL: The Tiananmen Square, they did it live on the air. You saw the Chinese. authorities go in and tell them to get out.

BRAZILE: Because they didn't want the story to get out, and so they banned the coverage.

I know this is a different -- a different incident, different all the way around, but the instincts are the same, in my judgment. The president wants to control the narrative. He wants to control the playbook.

And again, a week when the Chinese are coming, I think it's a bad timing.

KARL: Frank, why should Americans care whether or not reporters are allowed into the White House?

FRANK LUNTZ, POLLSTER & POLITICAL ANALYST: It's the right question. It's really not about what happens to the press. It's about what happens to the people. And it's more than just they're right. It's actually a responsibility.

One of my greatest concerns about democracy right now is that not enough people are paying attention or following the details, know the facts and know the truth. And anything that interrupts that delivery of truth from your profession to the American people, it should be opposed.

KARL: So, Erick, I want to ask you about something Ari Fleischer, of course, President Bush's former press secretary, and who's been very supportive of Trump on almost everything.

ERICK ERICKSON, “ERICK ERICKSON SHOW” HOST: Yeah. I think that's right. I mean, you had the situation with Fox News during the Obama administration that one time where the rest of the media stood up with Fox.

He has risen to power as a populist, in the sense that many working class people thought he was fighting for them.

KARL: He'd rather talk about those things (ph).

Those tend to work for the incumbent because they're known and the challengers aren't, but the economic variables with Iran and gas prices are hanging there for the Republicans to hurt them.

LUNTZ: And there's one problem here, which is turnout.

ERICKSON: Yes.

LUNTZ: The Republicans are just not activated to vote. And that's why the president held his session down in Texas. And it worked for a few days. And people don't remember. Jon, I've not seen a division in the generic ballot as big as it is right now.

KARL: Is this do you want to vote for a Democrat or a Republican for Congress?

LUNTZ: Correct. And it's over eight percent. Republicans cannot overcome that, even in redistricting challenges. And then you've got a turnout differential, which gives the Democrats a two percent advantage.

If I'm a Republican candidate right now, I'm absolutely back in my district. I'm back in my state because I know I got a lot of ground to catch up with.

BRAZILE: Jon, this spring, there were only four competitive Senate seats. We're now up to nine. We're talking about Alaska. We're talking about Texas, of course. These are ruby red states. Kansas, for example. The president --

KARL: Running as an Independent.

SHAKIR: Yeah, running as an Independent.

Angie Nixon, a very independent-minded legislator in Florida. Dahlia Rico, understood as a top versus bottom, not a left versus right candidate. Those things, those qualities are helping these candidates in a way that makes them step out in an environment in which you've already got the wins at your back.

KARL: How big an issue is artificial intelligence going to be?

SHAKIR: Oh, huge. Absolutely huge. Because it's bigger than just the issue of usage of A.I. It's a matter of who has wealth and power to control the decision-making of society. Who is in charge? It's a terrible messaging from these people.

KARL: Frank, quickly, how big an issue, you think?

SHAKIR: I think people are prepared to appreciate that we need borders, and we need enforcement. KARL: I mean, it's remarkable that Republicans have lost the advantage on immigration now.

ERICKSON: Yeah, it's just --

LUNTZ: It's a cultural battle. And he's referring back now 70 years. And it doesn't play with the American people who are looking at gas prices, who are looking at food prices and saying, what are you going to do for me right now? And I just -- I now -- I'm afraid that I didn't go to the Kennedy Center enough, that I missed this opportunity. But, Jon, in the end, it's all about a single attribute, truth.

The public has the right to know and the responsibility to learn this. And I'm urging members of Congress to adopt what I call the West Point Standard. You cannot lie, cheat, or steal, or tolerate those who do.

Could you imagine America right now?

KARL: I think that would be an interesting -- that would be a challenge for the Congress.

LUNTZ: Yes. And I'd love to see the -- they can't get involved in politics. They can't be partisan. They can't be political.

KARL: You're talking about your West Point Standards.

LUNTZ: But the West Point Standard --

KARL: Yeah.

LUNTZ: -- is what we need in America today.

SHAKIR: Well, we've got the politics of retribution. As you were saying, the poet, Martin Niemoller, at first they came for the communists, then they came for the socialists, then they came for the trade unions, they came for the Jews. This is the politics of the time we live in. And right now, there's a desire to divide us up and make us feel different than each other. In fact, hopefully, out of this era, in the darkness, we're seeing that we all share many things.

LUNTZ: Yes, but that's what you two do. And I'm so honored to be on this panel with the two of you. I've known you now for 25 years. I've known you for 15 years. The fact that you tell the truth here, that that is your highest standard, before politics, before partisanship, this is what America needs right now. And I thank you for what you've done.

BRAZILE: And look at ABC reuniting me with my old buddies from school.

KARL: All right.

(CROSSTALK)

BRAZILE: There you go.

(CROSSTALK)

news.title: Trump's approval rating drops, more voters say he's hurt the economy: new poll
news.text:
President Donald Trump's approval rating dropped in a new NBC News poll, and more voters criticized his handling of the economy, as the closely watched midterm elections approach.

Trump's approval rating hit a second-term low in the poll at 41% among registered voters, and 55% of voters said they think his policies have hurt the economy. The survey was released on Sept. 20.

In March, 48% of voters told NBC that they believe Trump has hurt the economy, and they ranked the cost of living as their most pressing issue facing the nation in March and September. NBC pollsters noted that the ongoing Iran war has driven up gasoline prices and other costs.

Trump says his triumphal arch will also serve as a 'military complex'

In all, Democrats in the latest survey wielded a 5-point lead in the battle for control of Congress – 50%-45% when respondents were asked who they'd prefer to control Capitol Hill. Still, that's down from their 12-point advantage in NBC polling at this point during the 2018 election cycle.

Democrats are also seen more negatively than Trump and the GOP, two years after former Vice President Kamala Harris lost the 2024 presidential race. Thirty-six percent of voters said they have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% said they have a negative view. Among Democrats, voters split 29% positive to 50% negative.

November's races are crucial for both parties as Democrats go on offense in a series of redder Senate races in states including Alaska, Iowa, Kansas North Carolina, Ohio and Texas. The party is also hoping to win back the House, which could be a roadblock for Trump: In the 2018 midterms, Democrats flipped the chamber in a "blue wave."

The incumbent president's party usually faces rough headwinds during midterm elections. NBC noted that Republicans trailed Democrats in the survey on who would better handle the key issue of inflation (31%-38%) and the economy (38%-39%). Additionally, more than 6 in 10 voters say the Iran war has not been worth it.

The NBC poll, which surveyed 1,000 registered voters via telephone and online from Sept. 11-15, has a margin of error of +/- three percentage points.

news.text:
Historical analogies are always dicey but hoo boy, with the state of the economy, the price of oil, and a new round of polling, Donald Trump is giving off serious Jimmy Carter vibes. 

I think Carter was a good president, but too many variables were out of his control, especially inflation. By the end of his term, it was over 10 percent. (It peaked at 13 percent in 1979.) Right or wrong, fair or not, he became known for inflation, or rather, for his inability to control it. 

Inflation is only 3.4 percent right now. There is a long way to go before we get to the Carter years. But Trump is on course. Not only is he unable to control it. He's actively pushing it up with a trio of bad choices: illegal deportations, illegal taxes and, especially, an illegal war. 

Carter faced oil shocks that drove up prices. Trump is causing oil shocks. The price of diesel broke records four days in a row. The price of gasoline is following suit. Those prices affect all prices, especially the cost of food. Just as everyone seemed mad at Carter, everyone seems mad at Trump. Disapproval of his handling of inflation is close to mainstream status.

A new Fox poll shows him 50 points underwater. A new Marquette University poll put that figure at 61 points. Not even Carter, whose presidency saw death by inflation, was that bad.

"Worse than Carter, worse than Reagan, worse than Biden," CNN's Harry Enten said. "He is worse than all three of those, and he is worse than any poll himself with this minus 61 points. 

"Literally, the worst of all time.

Inflation didn't just limit Jimmy Carter to one term. It discredited liberalism as a legitimate school of thought. Again, it's not really fair, because Jimmy Carter wasn't a liberal in terms of economic policy, but that's how he was portrayed by Ronald Reagan and his ideologues. 

Reagan ended liberalism's dominance in 1980, that year winning all but 6 states.

A consequence of their propaganda was the public image of the New Deal and Great Society – federal programs advancing liberty, equality and justice for all – being too expensive. Better to abandon them, or enervate them, and we did in time. All of us live in a world of Reagan's creation in which normal workaday Americans wade through thickets of red tape to get public assistance while the very obscenely rich get handouts with no strings attached. 

Carter's term was the turnbuckle. It was the end of one epoch – starting with the Great Depression and concluding with stagflation – and the beginning of another – starting with "supply-side economics" and concluding with whatever you want to call our current age of impunity and corruption. Eventually, it will have a name. In any case, it has the feel of an end-stage development. Something is going to break in this decade the way it broke in the 1970s. 

The question is will Trump be identified with that break the way Carter was?

I don't know, but obviously a lot will be determined by Trump. It is widely understood that he defeated Kamala Harris, because the electorate trusted him on inflation. (Inflation was in fact falling in 2024, but not fast enough to catch up with public opinion, which has been formed during the pandemic.) He would bring prices down on Day One, he said. Then he didn't. 

But not only has the president accelerated the already high cost of living with terrible choices. He won't take responsibility for them. Instead, he badgers voters into accepting inflation as the cost of ... well, no one is really sure. His reasons for attacking Iran have changed but the most often cited is preventing Iran from having a nuclear bomb. (Iran was not close to reaching that stage of development, but Trump can't be bothered with facts.) That goal, however, has not been enough even for his fiercest supporters, some of whom have taken to "begging" him on social media to end the war and bring diesel back to normal.

Carter has been on Trump's mind. In June, the Associated Press asked why he didn’t dispatch US Special Forces to remove Iran's uranium. “I didn’t feel like being Jimmy Carter," he replied. 

"That recalled the failed 1980 raid to free US hostages that killed eight American servicemen," the Associated Press reported in July. "Trump also said in March that the unsuccessful mission 'cost them the election' against Ronald Reagan in 1980, sounding cognizant of political realities in a way he didn’t when using Carter as a punchline."

Yet Trump faces a hostage crisis of his own, only he's the hostage. 

CBS News reported today the adviser to Iran's supreme leader said the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Trump and Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu are "removed from power." 

"Our fighters will not open the Strait of Hormuz until they bring the criminal Trump and the bloodthirsty Netanyahu down from the seat of power," said Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, the leading adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, according to Iranian state television.

Carter's choices did not cause inflation. Even so, he was blamed. Trump's choices did cause inflation. Voters now seem ready to blame him in such numbers that even Texas looks like it's ready to flip. A new Sienna poll suggests that James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate, is six points ahead of Republican Ken Paxton (49-43 percent), Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa is four points ahead of Republican Governor Greg Abbott (49-45 percent), and Democrats are nearly even in the generic ballot (Republicans' 47 percent to Democrats' 46 percent), which suggests an earthquake in the Texas legislature.

If that pattern held for two more years, and if the Democrats continued to make inroads, that would suggest another earthquake, this one national, as there is no path to victory for a Republican presidential candidate without 40 electoral votes from the Lone Star State.

No matter what happens in November's congressional elections, Trump will still be the president. He will still make terrible choices. And those choices will still push inflation up. (The Fed raised interest rates Wednesday and is expected to raise them again by year's end, but it might be a matter of too little, too late.) Two years is a very, very long time, long enough for Trump-blaming to become permanent, and long enough perhaps to discredit the maga movement and the ideological underpinnings of the last 45 years. The mainstream used to call "supply-side economics" a policy. By 2028, the mainstream might be calling it theft.

Trump's maga is the end-stage of Reagan's conservatism. 

If Texas is lost, that might be the end of both.

I have made these historical analogies before, and I have been wrong too many times to have too much confidence in them. That said, our moment does have a familiar ring to it. The politics of the late 2020s may be as pivotal historically as the politics of the late 1970s. Epochal transitions are usually triggered by crisis. I used to think that was the pandemic. I used to compare Trump's first term to Carter's. But, perhaps, the real crisis has always been covid's long tail of inflation. I don't want to get ahead of myself, but history is rhyming.

news.title: Susie Wiles is Trump’s chief enabler
news.text:
There are always power centers in any White House. Certain people have their own little fiefdoms or specific knowledge of how government bureaucracy works, which gives them a leg up in internecine battles. Some offices or Cabinet posts are just imbued with more power than others. The Treasury secretary, for example, is always going to have more juice than the secretary of agriculture, just by virtue of their respective portfolios. But there is no job that has traditionally been more powerful than White House chief of staff.

The role of the position is multi-faceted, managing the flow of information to the Oval Office and keeping them from becoming distracted by people pushing their own agendas and distorting the president’s understanding of the facts. The chief of staff has hiring and firing power over the West Wing, basically running the day-to-day operation of the presidency. Mediating disputes among the executive branch’s advisers and officials before they reach the president is also an important part of the job. But most importantly, the chief of staff should be the president’s most trusted adviser, willing to provide an honest assessment and opinion on all the important issues that reach the Resolute Desk. 

No president has a more checkered past with chiefs of staff than Donald Trump. In 2017, as a complete political novice, he brought in a GOP party hack, Reince Priebus, who quickly proved himself to be completely unprepared to deal with an egomaniac like Trump. Priebus was fairly swiftly given the heave-ho in favor of retired Gen. John Kelly, who was serving as secretary of homeland security. He was expected to whip the White House and the chaotic president into shape. While Kelly tried his best, he proved to be no match for the force that was Javanka — Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, the president’s son-in-law and daughter — and others who had forged a personal relationship with Trump and wielded influence, no matter how hard Kelly tried to discipline the operation. After the four-star general couldn’t tame the Trump White House, they ended up with a bucket of lukewarm chamomile tea by the name of Mark Meadows, who is probably best remembered as the man who sat on his couch scrolling through his phone while insurrectionists stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, simply saying the president wanted to be alone. 

“It used to be a fairly stiff competition for the worst chief of staff in history,” according to Chris Whipple, author of “The Gatekeepers,” the definitive book on the subject, “but Meadows absolutely owns it.” Still, there were others. Until Meadows, most people would have considered H.R. Haldeman, Richard Nixon’s very loyal chief of staff, to be the lowest rating. After all, Haldeman actually did time for his crimes in service of Nixon’s infamous abuses of power. George H.W. Bush’s right-hand man, John Sununu, was known to be a terrible manager and a terrible boss, while Don Regan, who served in the Reagan administration, handled the disastrous Iran-Contra scandal badly and alienated the very powerful Nancy Reagan, which in the end proved to be fatal to his employment in the West Wing. 

According to Whipple, the consensus is that Howard Baker, Reagan’s final chief of staff, and Dick Cheney, who served Gerald Ford, were considered competent, but the “gold standard” is James Baker, Reagan’s first chief, and Leon Panetta, who brought much-needed organization and discipline to the chaotic early days of Bill Clinton’s presidency. 

Susie Wiles, Trump’s current chief of staff, won’t be included in that pantheon, even though the president’s second term is a very different operation than the first. Following his loss to Joe Biden in 2020, Trump and his inner circle spent their four years in the wilderness figuring out what they wanted to do if they got back into power and devised a strategy to get it done. According to New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, authors of the book “Regime Change,” the massive leaks that characterized the first term have given way to a tightly controlled administration run by a group of devoted loyalists. Their fealty appears to be voluntary, and Wiles will no doubt be credited with maintaining discipline among the staff far better than those who served in the first Trump White House. But the job is about more than discipline, and on that scale, Wiles is little better than Meadows. 

As the first female chief of staff in history, she does deserve credit for running, along with Chris LaCivita, Trump’s successful 2024 campaign, an operation that, at least for him, was relatively professional and buttoned up. After his win against Vice President Kamala Harris, Wiles was the logical choice to follow him into the White House. She seems to have found the key to managing Trump, which is to not manage him at all. (One imagines his mother reached the same conclusion around the time he reportedly gave his second-grade music teacher a black eye because “he didn’t know anything about music.”) 

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Whipple interviewed Wiles eleven times for a major feature in Vanity Fair, and she was incredibly frank, letting it be known that she didn’t think much of Vice President JD Vance, characterizing him as an opportunist and a “conspiracy theorist.” She also called Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget — and the author of much of Project 2025 — a “right-wing absolute zealot.” But Wiles also revealed that she doesn’t see her job as one in which she tries to help the president sort through all the options and do the hard job of offering her unvarnished advice, even when it’s something Trump doesn’t want to hear.

Wiles denies that she is an enabler, but it’s clear that Vance was right when he told Whipple that she sees her job as a “facilitator,” which simply means that she makes sure the president’s disordered trains of thought run on time. She even more or less admitted it herself when she said that she only has difficult conversations with the boss over “little things.” Wiles revealed that she doesn’t have “these seminal moments where you have to go in and tell the president what he wants to do is unconstitutional or will cost lives. I don’t have that.” 

That pretty much says it all. And one has to question whether Wiles challenges him on the little things either. After all, in addition to a list of cronies and sycophants, Trump appointed her to the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. If she had any clout, you would think she could have talked him out of his petty obsession of adding his name to a living memorial to a revered, slain president — a disgusting act of desecration. But with Trump, there’s nothing too small on which to fixate and, in any case, this crusade to remake Washington, D.C., in his own image overwhelms all other concerns, including economic crises and war. 

In other words, Susie Wiles has no influence over Trump at all. Just like Mark Meadows, she’s essentially sitting on a couch and scrolling on her phone while the world burns.

news.title: Alaska’s Independent Streak Rears Its Head At The Wrong Moment For GOP
news.text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska – Scott Wheaton thinks a lot about why people vote the way they do in elections. He doesn’t work in politics; he’s a retired geologist. But sitting outside Dark Horse Coffee one sunny day earlier this month, Wheaton described himself as a “super voter” who takes elections very seriously, which is why he’s become fascinated by what makes someone ultimately pick one candidate over another.

“We vote for these bullshit reasons,” said Wheaton, 77, reclining in an Adirondack chair with a dog-eared book on his lap. “But I really think one of the big bullshit reasons we vote is we look at people and we say, ‘Do I like this person? Would I want this person to help me out?’”

That’s how he’s weighing his vote in Alaska’s Senate race, one of the most competitive in the country. Voters have a choice between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, the two-term incumbent, and his main challenger, Mary Peltola, a former Democratic representative. With the Senate teetering on the edge of flipping to Democratic control in November, Peltola is one of the Democrats poised to help her party potentially pull it off. She’s been narrowly leading in the polls for months and outperformed Sullivan in last month’s primary election.

To Wheaton, an independent voter and lifelong Alaskan, the choice in this race is obvious. All you have to do is look at them with fish.

“Mary’s splaying the fish, she’s drying the fish, she’s working at a drying rack, she’s working on clearly what’s a working boat. It’s dirty and grungy,” Wheaton said of Peltola’s campaign ad. “She’s just grungy, guys. We can tell she is. We can tell she’s a real person that does real work.”

Sullivan, meanwhile, is the guy who poses for a photo holding up a big fish, he said, and whose campaign is promoting a photo of him next to a dead bear he shot.

“For Dan Sullivan, it’s pasted on,” said Wheaton. “It’s like, ‘Oh, he shot a Kodiak bear?’ Give me a freakin’ break. It’s like he’s out shooting brown bears whenever he’s not being a senator? It’s just a stupid concept.”

Alaska is a red state. President Donald Trump won here in 2024 by 14 percentage points. But it’s also known for its sharp and proud independent streak. For some perspective on how much sway voters have here who aren’t registered Democrats or Republicans: 611,940 Alaskans voted in the 2024 presidential election. A 58% majority of them were registered as nonpartisan or undeclared.

I spent a few days talking to random Alaska voters, in grocery store parking lots in Anchorage and at the Alaska State Fair in the more conservative town of Palmer, a 45-minute drive north. I interviewed nearly four dozen Republicans, Democrats, independents and even someone in The Useless Clown Party (it’s a recognized political group here!). I asked the same questions of everyone — do you plan to vote in the Senate race, and if so, for whom and why? — spanning families, older couples, young adults and people of different genders and races.

Across the board, people shared how tired they are of division and chaos in politics. When they think about the Senate race, they said, they’re looking for someone who seems authentic, someone they could comfortably talk to, and someone they believe will put the public’s interests above their own. Democrats and Republicans mostly applied that criteria along party lines.

“I will vote for Sullivan,” said Tom of Anchorage, 65, a Republican voter who requested to only use his first name. “He’s committed to the Alaskan state. He’s committed to us.”

“Mary all the way. Don’t get me started on the other asshole,” said Rhonda Platt of Cordova, a port city with a population of about 2,600. A Democrat, Platt ripped Sullivan’s support for policies that have fueled high costs in her community — chief among them Trump’s war in Iran and economic tariffs on Canada.

“You’re talking to somebody who lives in a landlocked fishing village. A gallon of milk in Cordova is $15 a gallon. Gas is six bucks a gallon,” fumed Platt, 66. “For me, everything goes right back to Sullivan. I trust the dude as far as I can pick him up and throw him.”

“They’re in it for themselves,” she added. “I believe that Mary’s for Alaskans.”

Where things got more interesting is when independent voters weighed in. By and large, they said they want a relatable candidate who will look out for regular people instead of the rich and powerful — and concluded that Peltola is the better choice.

“I think she best represents Alaskan interests, and I think that Dan Sullivan is a snake,” said Liz Dennison, an independent voter in Anchorage.

Dennison, 66, knocked Sullivan as “a Trump mouthpiece” who isn’t even from Alaska (he’s originally from Ohio — the term “carpetbagger” came up in a few interviews), while Peltola seems “much more approachable” in her ads and at her live events.

Another independent voter in Anchorage, 75-year-old Linda, who requested to use only her first name, said all she knows is she’s not voting for Sullivan. She’s mostly been annoyed at the inundation of mailers, calls and texts from groups that have already spent tens of millions of dollars to sway Alaskan voters one way or another. Several residents described getting at least five calls a day from various groups on top of repeat text messages and brochures.

“All this crap mail, saying the same thing over and over and over again,” she grumbled. “Quit wasting your money on that and do something useful. Put that money towards the homeless.”

There’s still about a month and a half to go until the election, and understandably, some people are still learning about candidates. Natalia Keogh, an independent voter in Anchorage, is undecided but leaning toward Sullivan. “I like his politics better than Peltola,” said Keogh, 55. What does that mean? “I guess action,” she said.

She thinks it’s a bad idea that Trump is planning to come to Alaska to campaign with Sullivan, given his abysmal approval ratings. She voted for Trump in 2024, and is “absolutely not” happy with the last two years because “he didn’t follow through on any promises.”

Asked why she thinks she’ll support Sullivan despite her anger at Trump, given that the senator has been a strong supporter of the president and his policies, Keogh paused. 

“That’s a good question,” she said. “Maybe I’ll change my mind.”

Fish are a defining issue in this Senate race, too.

Commercial trawling, when industrial ships drag football-field-sized nets through the water or along the ocean floor to catch large quantities of certain fish, has driven billions of dollars into the state’s economy. But it’s come with high rates of “bycatch,” or other fish accidentally scooped up in the nets and later discarded, dead. This bycatch comes out to about 141 million pounds of marine life in Alaska being tossed every year, and includes fish like salmon and halibut, both vital to Indigenous communities that catch fish primarily for survival.

Combined with the negative effects of climate change, trawling has depleted Alaska’s salmon populations so badly that local and Native Alaskan villages are in crisis. A lot of the revenue from industrial trawlers flows to Seattle, too, further infuriating Alaskans who have long fished recreationally but say they’re not catching anything now.

Sullivan and Peltola have made this issue central to their campaigns. Sullivan touts his role in getting 63 bills signed into law over the last 12 years that he says have helped Alaskan fisheries, and has knocked Peltola for not getting any bills signed into law during her two-year House stint. He introduced a bill in June aimed at reining in bycatch, though it’s worth noting he’s also an ally to commercial trawlers and takes lots of campaign money from them.

Peltola, who is Native Alaskan and a former fishing boat captain, even has fish in her campaign slogan: “Fish, Family and Freedom.” She talks about the issue in a more personal way.

“As someone who grew up salmon fishing on the Kuskokwim River with my father, I know firsthand that fish is more than food – it’s central to our Alaska way of life,” she said in a June statement, laying out her plan to help the state’s fisheries. “That way of life is under attack and the fish that fill our freezers are becoming harder and harder to find thanks to out-of-state factory trawlers, excessive bycatch, and destruction of our fisheries.”

Peltola’s campaign declined multiple requests for an interview, citing a packed schedule. Sullivan’s campaign did not respond to requests to connect.

Instead, Peltola provided a statement when asked about voters’ concerns over access to fish.

“The salmon runs that fed generations of Alaskans are shadows of what they were, and the communities that depend on them are suffering,” the Alaska Democrat told HuffPost. “We need bold action to take on the rigged system in DC and save our fisheries, and that’s why I’m fighting to ban factory trawling and protect Alaska fishermen.”

Peltola also took a shot at Sullivan: “As Lower 48 factory trawlers destroy our fisheries, my opponent is taking their campaign cash and refusing to fight for real solutions in DC. I’ll fight to save our fish, deliver relief for our fishermen, and make sure Alaskans are the ones benefiting from our fish – not the Seattle trawl fleet and Lower 48 corporations.”

Alaska Natives comprise more than 13% of the state’s population, and many live in remote areas you can’t reach by car. Kelsey, 33, lives in Chickaloon, a Native village with a population of about 250. An outdoor educator, she said out-of-state trawlers have hurt local commercial and sport fishing in her community, but mostly subsistence fishing.

Kelsey, who was guzzling a smoothie at the Alaska State Fair as we talked, said this issue is key to her choice in the Senate race. She’s leaning toward supporting Peltola.

“I think that Dan Sullivan … has had more meetings with business for money that’s leaving the state,” said Kelsey, who didn’t give her last name and didn’t identify with any party. “It’s been pitched to me that Mary is more going to support, like, actual residents, whether we just have our residential fishing license or, like, a subsistence license.”

On the other side of the fair, Nick Hanson was flinging people 30 feet into the air.

A local celebrity, Hanson, known as “The Eskimo Ninja,” has competed 11 times on American Ninja Warrior, the show featuring athletes taking on difficult obstacle courses. An Alaska Native who lives in the village of Unalakleet, he was showing people how to do a “blanket toss,” a tradition in which a person is launched into the air by dozens of other people pulling on the edges of a large blanket made of sewn seal skins. Historically, Indigenous hunters have done this to get a high vantage point to spot whales or seals out at sea.

Hanson, 38, said he definitely plans to vote in November but doesn’t disclose who he votes for. But he was clear about his most important issue: “Trawling’s the biggest one,” he said. “Our subsistence lifestyle is the main thing that is most important to me, and we don’t have fish because of the trawling. ... We don’t have any king salmon.”

Asked why this hasn’t gotten better if people know it’s a big problem, Hanson said, “Because nobody does anything about it after they say they’re going to do something about it.”

The most dispiriting trend was hearing young people say they didn’t plan to vote and their reasons why not.

“Convenience to go voting,” said Layla, 23, bobbling a baby in her arms. “I work. I have a daughter. Also, I don’t like either party. I just feel like we’re given, like, two shits in a hand and told to choose between them.”

“It’s just not our kind of fight,” said Siu Dawson, 25, as he loaded up his car with groceries outside of a Walmart. “It’s hard doing a lot with so little time.”

Melanie Han, an Asian American woman heading into the same Walmart in Anchorage, said she’s not sure if she’ll vote and feels like it doesn’t matter anyway.

“No matter who runs for Alaska, it’s going down the drain,” said Han, 34. “I don’t really tune into it because I feel like it’s empty promises. I don’t think it’s gonna make a difference.”

Others a bit older than them said they’re likely to vote.

Lowell Button, 40, had just won third place in a beard contest at the state fair when he shared that he’d be supporting Sullivan. He’ll only vote if he’s home on Election Day, though, and his support is entirely tied to his belief that Republicans will protect his job in the oil and gas industry.

“Anytime a Democrat gets power, I get laid off,” said Button, a resident of Palmer, his new award dangling in his beard. Sullivan is “very pro-development.”

Lingering by the nearby Hoop ’n Hula Milk ’n Cookies, a cookie vendor with a space for hula hooping next to it, Alex Wilson, 41, said she’s “not impressed” with Sullivan. Wilson, a resident of Palmer, is registered with The Useless Clown Party, a progressive political group grounded in the idea that “the traditional political circus” has failed to serve the people.

She said she works a lot on the Yukon, and people there haven’t been allowed to fish for king salmon since 2018. That’s leading her to want to support Peltola in November.

“I imagine his stance on big corporate fisheries’ management is really detrimental to our Native populations,” Wilson said of Sullivan. “The villages are dying. My heart lies with the Indigenous populations. And so, Mary Peltola being an Indigenous woman is huge, in my mind.”

You can’t talk about this Senate race without talking about Dan Sullivan — the other Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

Alaska uses a “pick one” system of voting in its primaries, meaning people vote for a preferred candidate — regardless of party — and the top four vote-getters advance to the general election ballot in November, when voters used a ranked-choice system, ranking their favorite candidates in order. Peltola and Sen. Sullivan are the top two Senate candidates to advance after the August primary. The third candidate is the other Sullivan, a retired teacher on the island community of Petersburg. We’ll call him Teacher Sullivan.

Residents aren’t sure whether Teacher Sullivan is a plant or a genuinely frustrated Alaskan voter taking advantage of his name to make trouble for the current senator. An independent-turned-Republican, Teacher Sullivan is running to the left of Sen. Sullivan and has criticized his senator for being unresponsive to constituents.

Republican voters didn’t have much to say about the weird Dan Sullivan situation. Independents and Democrats said they loved it.

“I think it’s hilarious,” said Ryan Moldenhauer, 28, of Anchorage. “He’s Alaskan. He’s from Petersburg. Like, he has every right to run.”

“Sen. Sullivan’s pissed because his campaign materials say ‘Sullivan,’” Linda, the independent voter in Anchorage, cackled. “That’s why he’s pissed, is his campaign materials.”

Teacher Sullivan “respectfully” declined to be interviewed. “Hope you get some nice late summer weather in Anchorage,” he said in an email. “Can’t wait to hear what Eric Hafner has to say! :))”

Hafner, a registered Democrat currently serving time in federal prison in New York, advanced last month in the primary for Alaska’s House seat.

He did not respond to a request for comment.

You also can’t really talk about this Senate race without talking about Alaska’s other senator, Lisa Murkowski. She’s the senior GOP senator, known for her centrist positions and for standing up to Trump when virtually nobody else in her party does. She’s not up for reelection until 2028, but her name came up plenty of times in interviews with voters.

Several saw parallels between Murkowski and Peltola, both being centrist and strong women. Both previously crossed party lines to endorse each other in their Senate and House races, respectively, but in this Senate cycle, Murkowski is backing her party’s ticket.

“I feel like she’s a Democratic version of Lisa Murkowski,” said Chris, an independent voter and Palmer resident who was having a great time throwing back beers at the state fair with her self-described “lover.” Both said they might vote and, as is the case with Murkowski, they like that Peltola is “willing to cross party lines to get things done.”

Elizabeth Belanger, a 50-year-old Democrat in Anchorage, said she sees Peltola strategically appealing to the same mixed base of Democratic, independent and moderate Republican voters who routinely elect Murkowski.

“Peltola is running as a Democrat, but … I heard she turned down campaign contributions from Kamala Harris. Because she was like, ‘No, we’re not associating ourselves with the mainline Democrats,’” said Belanger, likely referring to Peltola this year rejecting unsolicited support from the former Democratic vice presidential nominee.

“That’s probably what’s helping her, you know?” she said.

“I love Lisa Murkowski,” offered Diana, 65, a conservative Republican in Anchorage. “She stands her ground. She votes what she thinks is right.”

A former engineer for BP, Diana said she and her husband vote the same in every election so they don’t cancel each other’s votes out. In November, they’ll “probably” support Sullivan, she said, because they don’t want Democrats to win control of the Senate.

But in what felt like a sudden flash of Alaskans’ libertarian streak, after about 10 minutes of talking, Diana seemed to want to support Peltola — and said not to tell her husband.

“Who can’t love Mary Peltola?” she added. Asked what the hell just happened in our conversation, Diana replied, “I said I didn’t think I was going to vote for her.”

“My son is going to vote for her,” Diana added. “He likes her.”

“We vote for these bullshit reasons,” said Wheaton, 77, reclining in an Adirondack chair with a dog-eared book on his lap. “But I really think one of the big bullshit reasons we vote is we look at people and we say, ‘Do I like this person? Would I want this person to help me out?’”

She’s been narrowly leading in the polls for months and outperformed Sullivan in last month’s primary election.

To Wheaton, an independent voter and lifelong Alaskan, the choice in this race is obvious. All you have to do is look at them with fish.

“Mary’s splaying the fish, she’s drying the fish, she’s working at a drying rack, she’s working on clearly what’s a working boat. It’s dirty and grungy,” Wheaton said of Peltola’s campaign ad. “She’s just grungy, guys. We can tell she is. We can tell she’s a real person that does real work.”

Sullivan, meanwhile, is the guy who poses for a photo holding up a big fish, he said, and whose campaign is promoting a photo of him next to a dead bear he shot.

“For Dan Sullivan, it’s pasted on,” said Wheaton. “It’s like, ‘Oh, he shot a Kodiak bear?’ Give me a freakin’ break. It’s like he’s out shooting brown bears whenever he’s not being a senator? It’s just a stupid concept.”

news.title: Republican Mike Rogers courts Michigan Democrats and Trump voters as GOP hopes to hold the Senate
news.text:
DETROIT (AP) — Mike Rogers stood outside Cody High School on Detroit’s west side on a recent drizzly morning and decried Michigan’s decline in reading achievement.

“This is the civil rights issue of our lifetime,” said the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in the open-seat race in November.

It had the look and sound of a Democratic campaign policy event, set in one of the nation’s Democratic-voting strongholds.

The contest has quickly become a focal point in the fight for Senate control, and Rogers is working to appeal to segments of Michigan’s Democratic electorate. It’s a key to what the former congressman sees as his path to defeating progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this fall.

Rogers lost his first bid for Senate two years ago by barely 19,000 votes out of more than 5.5 million cast. This time, he is betting he can win over some Democrats and independents, particularly Black and Jewish voters who may be turned off by El-Sayed’s positions, which are to the left of his party’s establishment, notably on U.S.-Israel relations. At the same time, Rogers must rally Donald Trump loyalists to turn out to vote, even though the president isn’t on the ballot.

“He is threading a needle,” said Bobby Schostak, Rogers’ campaign finance chairman.

Rogers is reaching into heavily Democratic Detroit

Rogers’ event outside Cody was part of his promotion of a nonprofit program to boost literacy in Michigan’s largest city. A few days later, he promoted a home construction plan in downtown Detroit, where many thousands of lots remain vacant almost 20 years after the Great Recession.

Rogers’ campaign sees opportunity in racially and culturally diverse Wayne County, home to Detroit, where roughly three-quarters of the population is Black.

In the 2024 Senate race, then-U.S. Rep. Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, won the county by more than a 2-to-1 margin over Rogers, or 264,000 votes. Squeezing even a couple more percentage points there in November could be enough for Rogers to win. His team is optimistic in part because in this year’s Democratic primary, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens beat El-Sayed in the county.

El-Sayed has faced resistance from some of Detroit’s older and more establishment-aligned Black Democrats, who favored Stevens’ longer-standing ties to Black churches and work on the Obama administration’s auto industry rescue plan.

Some local Black activists also faulted El-Sayed, who if elected would be the first Muslim senator, for supporting the “uncommitted” campaign in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary. Some Black Michigan Democrats believe the effort, aimed at pressuring the Biden administration over Gaza, cost then-Vice President Kamala Harris in her campaign as the first Black woman to be a major party presidential nominee. Trump beat Harris by 1.4 percentage points in the state.

Harris plans to campaign with El-Sayed in Michigan on Tuesday, and the Congressional Black Caucus has endorsed El-Sayed.

Democratic leaders have dismissed Rogers’ efforts at inroads.

“I don’t think anyone’s buying it,” the state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said of Rogers’ efforts to court Black voters in Detroit. “I don’t think (Rogers) has a connection in those communities, I think he’s going to have a hard time.”

Some Jewish Democrats are siding with Rogers

Rogers has also leaned into the defections by some Democratic Jewish voters, an influential group particularly in Oakland County, Michigan’s second most-populous county.

A day after the August primary, a prominent Democrat, Detroit-area business leader Brian Hermelin, called Schostak, Rogers’ campaign finance chairman, asking how he could help. Within 10 days, Rogers was headlining a fundraiser hosted by the Hermelin family and attended by about 130 people, mostly Democrats, Schostak said.

El-Sayed opposes U.S. military aid to Israel and has called the U.S. ally’s military campaign in Gaza a “genocide,” an accusation rejected by the Israeli and U.S. governments. The former public health official also has angered some Jewish Democrats with statements he made after the March attack on Temple Israel, Michigan’s largest Jewish congregation.

El-Sayed’s suggestion that “hurt people hurt people” was interpreted by some as justification for the attack. El-Sayed later apologized for his response, but the remark helped push some influential Jewish Democrats toward Rogers.

Oakland County commercial real estate broker Benji Rosenzweig, who is Jewish and tends to vote for Democrats, plans to vote for the Republican.

“As a Jew, my family doesn’t feel safe with Abdul El-Sayed,” Rosenzweig said.

Michigan is a potential Republican firewall

The seat is open because Democrat Gary Peters is not seeking reelection. If Rogers wins, Republicans would retain their Senate majority even if Democrats pick up as many as four GOP-held seats in November.

Ad spending reflects the stakes. More money has been spent in Michigan — almost $125 million since the Aug. 4 primary — than in any other state where Republicans have a chance at gaining a seat, according to the advertising-tracking firm AdImpact. That is spending by El-Sayed, Rogers and allied groups.

The race has jumped to the top of the Trump political team’s priority list.

No Going Back, a new entity linked to Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC, early this month spent $18.5 million to air ads and reserve advertising time in Michigan, the most the group has committed to any 2026 Senate race so far, according to AdImpact.

The ads show the split-screen tack Rogers and his allies are taking in reaching out to atypical Republican voters while working to inspire the Trump base.

Rogers’ campaign organization is airing ads, many of them with him direct to camera, promoting him as the son of a middle-class family, a collaborator during his time in Congress and interested in bringing down costs, notably for healthcare.

The super PACs supporting his candidacy are swinging the hammer. For instance, the super PAC associated with GOP Senate leadership is airing ads noting El-Sayed’s past association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker and the candidate’s support for abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rogers has walked a fine line on Trump

The division of messaging reflects that Rogers’ team is wary of Trump’s low approval, especially on handling the economy, and wants to be seen among the broad swath of Michigan voters as not beholden to the president.

As he says in one ad, “Michigan comes first.”

Yet he has shifted closer to Trump.

After the 2020 election, Rogers was unequivocal that Democrat Joe Biden defeated Trump for the White House, and Rogers he criticized Trump’s unfounded claims of widespread fraud. But in July, after Trump’s primetime address recycling the disproven claims, Rogers praised Trump’s “commitment to transparency.”

He has not shied away from the rhetoric that appeals to Trump’s supporters, but delivers it in a less edgy tone.

Speaking to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, Rogers referenced “radical Islamic terrorism.” He also said El-Sayed had “chosen Hasan Piker as his running mate.”

Piker, who in 2019 said the U.S. “deserved 9/11,” had hosted El-Sayed on his livestream and later campaigned with him at rallies during the primary. El-Sayed has since disavowed Piker’s controversial statements and ended plans for joint campaigning, but has not categorically repudiated him nor apologized for appearing with him.

Not once during Rogers’ convention speech did he mention Trump, as so many speakers did over the two-night event.

Instead, Rogers closed by echoing a quote attributed to Michigan native Todd Beamer, among the passengers aboard United Flight 93 before its crash in Pennsylvania on Sept. 11.

Jabbing a finger toward the audience, Rogers said, “America, let’s roll.”

Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Nicholas Riccardi in Grand Rapids, Mich., contributed to this report.
